raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: Why this story matters — the gap between flying-as-airline-passenger and flying-as-private-pilot
raw_evidence.content: U.S. commercial aviation is one of the safest forms of transportation ever engineered: the airlines have flown for years on end without a passenger fatality in the U.S. General aviation is a different story. A private pilot in a Cessna 172 is operating in a regulatory regime, training environment, weather-decision context, and maintenance economy that is meaningfully closer to driving a car than to riding on Delta. The gap matters for two reasons. First, it shapes public perception: small-plane crashes generate disproportionate local-news coverage relative to airline accidents because they are common enough to be regular and rare enough to still be newsworthy. Second, the regulatory and educational levers that fixed airline safety in the 1990s and 2000s (crew resource management, sophisticated simulator training, two-pilot crews, mandatory route planning) only partly map onto single-pilot light-aircraft operations. So the story this dataset can tell — what kills private pilots, where, in what airplanes, in what weather — is also the story of a safety problem that the easy fixes have already been applied to and which remains stubbornly resistant to the next wave of fixes.

raw_evidence.label: Probable-cause keyword taxonomy — what investigators actually say killed people
raw_evidence.content: Mining the 17,254 events with NTSB-written probable-cause text (98.5% coverage) for canonical accident-pattern keywords gives a fatality-weighted ranking that closely matches the GA-safety-literature consensus (det_06). Loss of control: 1,646 events / 51.2% fatal / 1,431 deaths. Aerodynamic stall: 1,420 / 49.9% fatal / 1,179 deaths. Engine failure: 3,876 events / 12.7% fatal / 732 deaths (very common but mostly survivable). Spatial disorientation: 298 events / 95.0% fatal / 558 deaths — the highest fatality rate of any high-volume pattern, almost always lethal. Controlled flight into terrain: 103 / 84.5% / 169. Structural failure / in-flight breakup: 97 / 85.6% / 168. Alcohol or drug impairment: 161 / 82.0% / 194. Stall-spin combined: 235 / 82.1% / 313. The pattern is consistent: rare events kill almost everyone they touch (disorientation, structural failure, alcohol), common events kill a minority (engine failure, landing accidents).
raw_evidence.code:
"spin": r"\bspin(s|ned|ning)?\b",
    "fuel_exhaustion": r"fuel exhaustion|exhausted (?:the )?fuel|out of fuel",
    "fuel_starvation": r"fuel starvation|starved of fuel",
    "fuel_management": r"fuel (?:mis)?management|inadequate fuel",
    "engine_failure": r"engine failure|loss of engine power|partial loss of engine|engine malfunction",
    "vfr_into_imc": r"vfr (?:flight )?into (?:imc|instrument)|continued vfr flight into|continued visual flight into imc",
    "spatial_disorientation": r"spatial disorientation",
    "controlled_flight_into_terrain": r"controlled flight into terrain|cfit",
    "wire_strike": r"wire strike|struck (?:a |the )?wire|powerline",
    "bird_strike": r"bird strike|struck a bird",
    "icing": r"\bicing\b|airframe ice|carb(?:uretor)? ice",
    "go_around": r"go.?around",
    "runway_excursion": r"runway excursion|departed the runway|overran the runway|veered off the runway",
    "hard_landing": r"hard landing",
    "porpoise": r"porpois(e|ing)",
    "stall_spin": r"stall(\b.{0,20}\bspin)|stall/spin",
    "improper_decision": r"improper (?:decision|judgment)|inadequate decision",
    "pilot_inexperience": r"inexperience(?:d)?|insufficient (?:total )?experience",
    "alcohol_drugs": r"alcohol|impairment|drug",
    "midair_collision": r"mid.?air collision|midair collision",
    "structural_failure": r"structural failure|in.?flight breakup|in.?flight break.?up",
    # Phases recovered from text — recovers what phase_flt_spec lost:
    "phase_takeoff": r"\b(takeoff|take.?off|initial climb)\b",
    "phase_landing": r"\b(landing|touchdown|flare)\b",
    "phase_approach": r"\bapproach\b",
    "phase_cruise": r"\bcruise\b",
    "phase_maneuvering": r"\bmaneuver(?:ing|ed)?\b",
    "phase_taxi": r"\btaxi(?:ing|ed)?\b",
}

# Roll one row per event (use first non-null cause text per event).
ev = df.groupby("ev_id").agg(
    cause=("cause_lc", "first"),
    fatal=("fatal", "any"),
    deaths=("inj_tot_f", "max"),
).reset_index()
total_events = ev.shape[0]
events_with_cause = ev[ev["cause"].str.len() > 0]
total_with_cause = events_with_cause.shape[0]
print(f"events_total: {total_events}")
print(f"events_with_cause_text: {total_with_cause}")
print(f"cause_text_coverage_pct: {total_with_cause / total_events * 100:.1f}")

rows = []
for name, pat in patterns.items():
    rx = re.compile(pat)
    hit = events_with_cause["cause"].str.contains(rx, regex=True)
    n = int(hit.sum())
    fatal_n = int(events_with_cause.loc[hit, "fatal"].sum())
    deaths = int(events_with_cause.loc[hit, "deaths"].sum())
    pct = (n / total_with_cause * 100) if total_with_cause else 0.0
    fpct = (fatal_n / n * 100) if n else 0.0
    rows.append({
        "pattern": name,
        "events": n,
        "events_pct": round(pct, 1),
        "fatal_events": fatal_n,
        "fatal_share_pct": round(fpct, 1),
        "deaths_sum": deaths,
    })

cause_tbl = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("events", ascending=False)
print(cause_tbl.to_string(index=False))

# --- ana_21: VFR-into-IMC by text vs by columns (cross-check det_05) ---
print("=== ana_21 ===")
text_hits = events_with_cause["cause"].str.contains(r"vfr (?:flight )?into (?:imc|instrument)|continued vfr flight into|continued visual flight into imc", regex=True)

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: Why this story matters — the gap between flying-as-airline-passenger and flying-as-private-pilot
raw_evidence.content: U.S. commercial aviation is one of the safest forms of transportation ever engineered: the airlines have flown for years on end without a passenger fatality in the U.S. General aviation is a different story. A private pilot in a Cessna 172 is operating in a regulatory regime, training environment, weather-decision context, and maintenance economy that is meaningfully closer to driving a car than to riding on Delta. The gap matters for two reasons. First, it shapes public perception: small-plane crashes generate disproportionate local-news coverage relative to airline accidents because they are common enough to be regular and rare enough to still be newsworthy. Second, the regulatory and educational levers that fixed airline safety in the 1990s and 2000s (crew resource management, sophisticated simulator training, two-pilot crews, mandatory route planning) only partly map onto single-pilot light-aircraft operations. So the story this dataset can tell — what kills private pilots, where, in what airplanes, in what weather — is also the story of a safety problem that the easy fixes have already been applied to and which remains stubbornly resistant to the next wave of fixes.

raw_evidence.content: Mining the 17,254 events with NTSB-written probable-cause text (98.5% coverage) for canonical accident-pattern keywords gives a fatality-weighted ranking that closely matches the GA-safety-literature consensus (det_06). Loss of control: 1,646 events / 51.2% fatal / 1,431 deaths. Aerodynamic stall: 1,420 / 49.9% fatal / 1,179 deaths. Engine failure: 3,876 events / 12.7% fatal / 732 deaths (very common but mostly survivable). Spatial disorientation: 298 events / 95.0% fatal / 558 deaths — the highest fatality rate of any high-volume pattern, almost always lethal. Controlled flight into terrain: 103 / 84.5% / 169. Structural failure / in-flight breakup: 97 / 85.6% / 168. Alcohol or drug impairment: 161 / 82.0% / 194. Stall-spin combined: 235 / 82.1% / 313. The pattern is consistent: rare events kill almost everyone they touch (disorientation, structural failure, alcohol), common events kill a minority (engine failure, landing accidents).

"spin": r"\bspin(s|ned|ning)?\b",
    "fuel_exhaustion": r"fuel exhaustion|exhausted (?:the )?fuel|out of fuel",

    "fuel_management": r"fuel (?:mis)?management|inadequate fuel",
    "engine_failure": r"engine failure|loss of engine power|partial loss of engine|engine malfunction",
    "vfr_into_imc": r"vfr (?:flight )?into (?:imc|instrument)|continued vfr flight into|continued visual flight into imc",

    "wire_strike": r"wire strike|struck (?:a |the )?wire|powerline",
    "bird_strike": r"bird strike|struck a bird",
    "icing": r"\bicing\b|airframe ice|carb(?:uretor)? ice",
    "go_around": r"go.?around",
    "runway_excursion": r"runway excursion|departed the runway|overran the runway|veered off the runway",
    "hard_landing": r"hard landing",
    "porpoise": r"porpois(e|ing)",
    "stall_spin": r"stall(\b.{0,20}\bspin)|stall/spin",
    "improper_decision": r"improper (?:decision|judgment)|inadequate decision",
    "pilot_inexperience": r"inexperience(?:d)?|insufficient (?:total )?experience",
    "alcohol_drugs": r"alcohol|impairment|drug",
    "midair_collision": r"mid.?air collision|midair collision",
    "structural_failure": r"structural failure|in.?flight breakup|in.?flight break.?up",
    # Phases recovered from text — recovers what phase_flt_spec lost:
    "phase_takeoff": r"\b(takeoff|take.?off|initial climb)\b",
    "phase_landing": r"\b(landing|touchdown|flare)\b",
    "phase_approach": r"\bapproach\b",
    "phase_cruise": r"\bcruise\b",
    "phase_maneuvering": r"\bmaneuver(?:ing|ed)?\b",
    "phase_taxi": r"\btaxi(?:ing|ed)?\b",
}

# Roll one row per event (use first non-null cause text per event).
ev = df.groupby("ev_id").agg(
    cause=("cause_lc", "first"),
    fatal=("fatal", "any"),
    deaths=("inj_tot_f", "max"),
).reset_index()
total_events = ev.shape[0]
events_with_cause = ev[ev["cause"].str.len() > 0]
total_with_cause = events_with_cause.shape[0]
print(f"events_total: {total_events}")
print(f"events_with_cause_text: {total_with_cause}")
print(f"cause_text_coverage_pct: {total_with_cause / total_events * 100:.1f}")

rows = []
for name, pat in patterns.items():
    rx = re.compile(pat)
    hit = events_with_cause["cause"].str.contains(rx, regex=True)
    n = int(hit.sum())

    rows.append({
        "pattern": name,
        "events": n,
        "events_pct": round(pct, 1),
        "fatal_events": fatal_n,
        "fatal_share_pct": round(fpct, 1),
        "deaths_sum": deaths,
    })

cause_tbl = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("events", ascending=False)
print(cause_tbl.to_string(index=False))

# --- ana_21: VFR-into-IMC by text vs by columns (cross-check det_05) ---
print("=== ana_21 ===")
text_hits = events_with_cause["cause"].str.contains(r"vfr (?:flight )?into (?:imc|instrument)|continued vfr flight into|continued visual flight into imc", regex=True)

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: Why this story matters — the gap between flying-as-airline-passenger and flying-as-private-pilot
raw_evidence.content: U.S. commercial aviation is one of the safest forms of transportation ever engineered: the airlines have flown for years on end without a passenger fatality in the U.S. General aviation is a different story. A private pilot in a Cessna 172 is operating in a regulatory regime, training environment, weather-decision context, and maintenance economy that is meaningfully closer to driving a car than to riding on Delta. The gap matters for two reasons. First, it shapes public perception: small-plane crashes generate disproportionate local-news coverage relative to airline accidents because they are common enough to be regular and rare enough to still be newsworthy. Second, the regulatory and educational levers that fixed airline safety in the 1990s and 2000s (crew resource management, sophisticated simulator training, two-pilot crews, mandatory route planning) only partly map onto single-pilot light-aircraft operations. So the story this dataset can tell — what kills private pilots, where, in what airplanes, in what weather — is also the story of a safety problem that the easy fixes have already been applied to and which remains stubbornly resistant to the next wave of fixes.

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: Why this story matters — the gap between flying-as-airline-passenger and flying-as-private-pilot
raw_evidence.content: U.S. commercial aviation is one of the safest forms of transportation ever engineered: the airlines have flown for years on end without a passenger fatality in the U.S. General aviation is a different story. A private pilot in a Cessna 172 is operating in a regulatory regime, training environment, weather-decision context, and maintenance economy that is meaningfully closer to driving a car than to riding on Delta. The gap matters for two reasons. First, it shapes public perception: small-plane crashes generate disproportionate local-news coverage relative to airline accidents because they are common enough to be regular and rare enough to still be newsworthy. Second, the regulatory and educational levers that fixed airline safety in the 1990s and 2000s (crew resource management, sophisticated simulator training, two-pilot crews, mandatory route planning) only partly map onto single-pilot light-aircraft operations. So the story this dataset can tell — what kills private pilots, where, in what airplanes, in what weather — is also the story of a safety problem that the easy fixes have already been applied to and which remains stubbornly resistant to the next wave of fixes.

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: Why this story matters — the gap between flying-as-airline-passenger and flying-as-private-pilot
raw_evidence.content: U.S. commercial aviation is one of the safest forms of transportation ever engineered: the airlines have flown for years on end without a passenger fatality in the U.S. General aviation is a different story. A private pilot in a Cessna 172 is operating in a regulatory regime, training environment, weather-decision context, and maintenance economy that is meaningfully closer to driving a car than to riding on Delta. The gap matters for two reasons. First, it shapes public perception: small-plane crashes generate disproportionate local-news coverage relative to airline accidents because they are common enough to be regular and rare enough to still be newsworthy. Second, the regulatory and educational levers that fixed airline safety in the 1990s and 2000s (crew resource management, sophisticated simulator training, two-pilot crews, mandatory route planning) only partly map onto single-pilot light-aircraft operations. So the story this dataset can tell — what kills private pilots, where, in what airplanes, in what weather — is also the story of a safety problem that the easy fixes have already been applied to and which remains stubbornly resistant to the next wave of fixes.

raw_evidence.label: Probable-cause keyword taxonomy — what investigators actually say killed people
raw_evidence.content: Mining the 17,254 events with NTSB-written probable-cause text (98.5% coverage) for canonical accident-pattern keywords gives a fatality-weighted ranking that closely matches the GA-safety-literature consensus (det_06). raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: Why this story matters — the gap between flying-as-airline-passenger and flying-as-private-pilot
raw_evidence.content: U.S. commercial aviation is one of the safest forms of transportation ever engineered: the airlines have flown for years on end without a passenger fatality in the U.S. General aviation is a different story. A private pilot in a Cessna 172 is operating in a regulatory regime, training environment, weather-decision context, and maintenance economy that is meaningfully closer to driving a car than to riding on Delta. The gap matters for two reasons. First, it shapes public perception: small-plane crashes generate disproportionate local-news coverage relative to airline accidents because they are common enough to be regular and rare enough to still be newsworthy. Second, the regulatory and educational levers that fixed airline safety in the 1990s and 2000s (crew resource management, sophisticated simulator training, two-pilot crews, mandatory route planning) only partly map onto single-pilot light-aircraft operations. So the story this dataset can tell — what kills private pilots, where, in what airplanes, in what weather — is also the story of a safety problem that the easy fixes have already been applied to and which remains stubbornly resistant to the next wave of fixes.

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: Why this story matters — the gap between flying-as-airline-passenger and flying-as-private-pilot
raw_evidence.content: U.S. commercial aviation is one of the safest forms of transportation ever engineered: the airlines have flown for years on end without a passenger fatality in the U.S. General aviation is a different story. A private pilot in a Cessna 172 is operating in a regulatory regime, training environment, weather-decision context, and maintenance economy that is meaningfully closer to driving a car than to riding on Delta. The gap matters for two reasons. First, it shapes public perception: small-plane crashes generate disproportionate local-news coverage relative to airline accidents because they are common enough to be regular and rare enough to still be newsworthy. Second, the regulatory and educational levers that fixed airline safety in the 1990s and 2000s (crew resource management, sophisticated simulator training, two-pilot crews, mandatory route planning) only partly map onto single-pilot light-aircraft operations. So the story this dataset can tell — what kills private pilots, where, in what airplanes, in what weather — is also the story of a safety problem that the easy fixes have already been applied to and which remains stubbornly resistant to the next wave of fixes.

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: Why this story matters — the gap between flying-as-airline-passenger and flying-as-private-pilot
raw_evidence.content: U.S. commercial aviation is one of the safest forms of transportation ever engineered: the airlines have flown for years on end without a passenger fatality in the U.S. General aviation is a different story. A private pilot in a Cessna 172 is operating in a regulatory regime, training environment, weather-decision context, and maintenance economy that is meaningfully closer to driving a car than to riding on Delta. The gap matters for two reasons. First, it shapes public perception: small-plane crashes generate disproportionate local-news coverage relative to airline accidents because they are common enough to be regular and rare enough to still be newsworthy. Second, the regulatory and educational levers that fixed airline safety in the 1990s and 2000s (crew resource management, sophisticated simulator training, two-pilot crews, mandatory route planning) only partly map onto single-pilot light-aircraft operations. So the story this dataset can tell — what kills private pilots, where, in what airplanes, in what weather — is also the story of a safety problem that the easy fixes have already been applied to and which remains stubbornly resistant to the next wave of fixes.

The pattern is consistent: rare events kill almost everyone they touch (disorientation, structural failure, alcohol), common events kill a minority (engine failure, landing accidents).

raw_evidence.label: NTSB Aviation Accident Database — origin and scope
raw_evidence.content: The dataset is the National Transportation Safety Board's complete, public Aviation Accident Database. The NTSB is an independent U.S. federal agency whose primary statutory mission is 'to determine the probable cause of transportation accidents and incidents and to formulate safety recommendations to improve transportation safety.' For aviation, the database goes back to 1962 and covers every civil aviation accident or selected incident inside the United States, its territories, and international waters where U.S. carriers were involved. Each row is the formal investigative output of a federal accident investigation: investigators arrive on scene, collect physical and documentary evidence, interview witnesses and survivors, examine wreckage, pull weather and air-traffic data, and ultimately publish a probable-cause finding. The 'narratives' columns in our slice (narr_accp, narr_accf, narr_cause) are the actual paragraphs investigators wrote — they are not summaries we have constructed but the agency's own words. This makes the dataset rare among public-domain records: every event is paired with a primary-source qualitative explanation written by a federal investigator with cause to be careful.

raw_evidence.label: What 'FAR Part 91' means — and why our slice excludes the airlines
raw_evidence.content: The data is filtered to far_part = '091', which is the NTSB code for flights conducted under 14 CFR Part 91 — the U.S. federal regulations covering general operating and flight rules for non-commercial flying. In plain English, Part 91 is the private side of American aviation: a single owner-pilot taking a Cessna 172 up on a Saturday, a flight school's training circuits, a doctor commuting home from a fishing trip in a Bonanza, two friends in a homebuilt RV-6 making a $100 hamburger run. It explicitly excludes the airlines (Part 121, which covers United, Delta, Southwest, etc.), commuter and on-demand carriers like medical evacuation under Part 135, agricultural crop-dusters under Part 137, and foreign carriers operating under Part 129. The narrative consequence is significant. Part 121 (the airlines) has gone two decades with essentially zero passenger fatalities on U.S. soil; Part 91 has not. Almost every fatal small-aircraft crash a reader sees on the local news happens under Part 91, and the question the dataset implicitly asks is: how dangerous, exactly, is it to fly as a private pilot, and what kills the most people who do?

The 'narratives' columns in our slice (narr_accp, narr_accf, narr_cause) are the actual paragraphs investigators wrote — they are not summaries we have constructed but the agency's own words. This makes the dataset rare among public-domain records: every event is paired with a primary-source qualitative explanation written by a federal investigator with cause to be careful.

raw_evidence.label: What 'FAR Part 91' means — and why our slice excludes the airlines
raw_evidence.content: The data is filtered to far_part = '091', which is the NTSB code for flights conducted under 14 CFR Part 91 — the U.S. federal regulations covering general operating and flight rules for non-commercial flying. In plain English, Part 91 is the private side of American aviation: a single owner-pilot taking a Cessna 172 up on a Saturday, a flight school's training circuits, a doctor commuting home from a fishing trip in a Bonanza, two friends in a homebuilt RV-6 making a $100 hamburger run. It explicitly excludes the airlines (Part 121, which covers United, Delta, Southwest, etc.), commuter and on-demand carriers like medical evacuation under Part 135, agricultural crop-dusters under Part 137, and foreign carriers operating under Part 129. The narrative consequence is significant. Part 121 (the airlines) has gone two decades with essentially zero passenger fatalities on U.S. soil; Part 91 has not. Almost every fatal small-aircraft crash a reader sees on the local news happens under Part 91, and the question the dataset implicitly asks is: how dangerous, exactly, is it to fly as a private pilot, and what kills the most people who do?

raw_evidence.label: Aircraft-category distribution — 88% are fixed-wing airplanes
raw_evidence.content: The GA fleet in this slice is overwhelmingly fixed-wing airplanes: 87.8% (15,555 rows). Helicopters are 7.1% (1,262), gliders 1.9% (344), balloons 0.9% (162), weight-shift / trike 0.8% (145), gyrocopters 0.8% (140), powered parachutes 0.5% (81), ultralights and others combined < 0.2%. The story should focus on fixed-wing because of statistical mass, but the helicopter slice is large enough (~84 events per year) to deserve its own callout for readers who think of 'small aircraft accidents' as mostly heli.

raw_evidence.label: NTSB Aviation Accident Database — origin and scope
raw_evidence.content: The dataset is the National Transportation Safety Board's complete, public Aviation Accident Database. The NTSB is an independent U.S. federal agency whose primary statutory mission is 'to determine the probable cause of transportation accidents and incidents and to formulate safety recommendations to improve transportation safety.' For aviation, the database goes back to 1962 and covers every civil aviation accident or selected incident inside the United States, its territories, and international waters where U.S. carriers were involved. Each row is the formal investigative output of a federal accident investigation: investigators arrive on scene, collect physical and documentary evidence, interview witnesses and survivors, examine wreckage, pull weather and air-traffic data, and ultimately publish a probable-cause finding. The 'narratives' columns in our slice (narr_accp, narr_accf, narr_cause) are the actual paragraphs investigators wrote — they are not summaries we have constructed but the agency's own words. This makes the dataset rare among public-domain records: every event is paired with a primary-source qualitative explanation written by a federal investigator with cause to be careful.

raw_evidence.label: Type of flying — personal flying dominates, instructional is safest
raw_evidence.content: Personal flying (PERS) is the activity in 72% of events (12,677). Its fatal share is 19.3% — close to the dataset average. The clean comparison the data forces is with instructional flying (INST): 2,734 events, but only 9.5% fatal — about half the personal-flying rate. Two readings of that gap, both true: training environments are deliberately safer (CFI on board, conservative weather minimums, restricted maneuvers); and personal flying is where pilots make the high-stakes weather-and-route decisions that lead to LOC-I and VFR-into-IMC. Air-show flying is rare (81 events) but has the highest fatal share of any meaningful category at 42.0%, consistent with low-altitude aerobatic display being among the most dangerous things you can do in a small airplane.
raw_evidence.code:
type_map = {
    "PERS": "Personal",
    "INST": "Instructional",
    "BUS": "Business",
    "BUS ": "Business",
    "EXEC": "Business",
    "FERY": "Ferry",
    "POSI": "Positioning",
    "OWRK": "Other-work",
    "GLDT": "Glider-tow",
    "AOBV": "Aerial-obs",
    "SKYD": "Skydiving",
    "BANT": "Banner-tow",
    "AAPL": "Aerial-app",
    "PUBF": "Public",
    "PUBS": "Public",
    "PUBL": "Public",
    "PUBU": "Public",
    "ASHO": "Air-show",
    "FIRF": "Firefighting",
    "FLTS": "Flight-test",
    "EXLD": "External-load",
    "ADRP": "Airdrop",
    "UNK": "Unknown",
    "UNK ": "Unknown",
}
df["flight_type"] = df["type_fly"].map(type_map).fillna("Other")
ft = df.groupby("flight_type").agg(events=("ev_id", "nunique"), fatal_events=("fatal", "sum")).reset_index()
ft["fatal_share_pct"] = (ft.fatal_events / ft.events * 100).round(1)
ft = ft.sort_values("events", ascending=False)
raw_evidence.output:
flight_type  events  fatal_events  fatal_share_pct
     Personal   12677          2441             19.3
Instructional    2734           261              9.5
     Business     516           103             20.0
  Positioning     379            81             21.4
  Flight-test     268            53             19.8
   Other-work     254            48             18.9
   Aerial-obs     253            55             21.7
        Ferry     100            15             15.0
    Skydiving      93            15             16.1
     Air-show      81            34             42.0

raw_evidence.label: Type of flying — personal flying dominates, instructional is safest
raw_evidence.content: Personal flying (PERS) is the activity in 72% of events (12,677). Its fatal share is 19.3% — close to the dataset average. The clean comparison the data forces is with instructional flying (INST): 2,734 events, but only 9.5% fatal — about half the personal-flying rate. Two readings of that gap, both true: training environments are deliberately safer (CFI on board, conservative weather minimums, restricted maneuvers); and personal flying is where pilots make the high-stakes weather-and-route decisions that lead to LOC-I and VFR-into-IMC. Air-show flying is rare (81 events) but has the highest fatal share of any meaningful category at 42.0%, consistent with low-altitude aerobatic display being among the most dangerous things you can do in a small airplane.

raw_evidence.label: Benchmark — GA fatal accident rate per 100,000 flight hours
raw_evidence.content: To make any sense of raw accident counts you need a flight-hours denominator. The FAA's annual General Aviation and Part 135 Activity Survey is the canonical source. The headline number to anchor on: the GA fatal accident rate has spent the last two decades drifting between roughly 0.65 and 1.40 fatal accidents per 100,000 flight hours. NBAA reported preliminary 2020 GA data at 1.049 fatal accidents per 100,000 hours, a 20-year low at the time, down from 1.274 in 2001 and a peak of 1.381 in 2005. By 2023 the figure had fallen further to about 0.65 per 100,000 flight hours, with 186 fatal accidents from 1,097 total. For comparison: U.S. Part 121 airline operations are essentially zero on the same scale. So the long-run story is: GA flying is slowly getting safer, but its fatal accident rate is still on the order of a hundred times worse than airline flying.

raw_evidence.content: To make any sense of raw accident counts you need a flight-hours denominator. The FAA's annual General Aviation and Part 135 Activity Survey is the canonical source. raw_evidence.label: VFR into IMC — the '178 seconds' problem
raw_evidence.content: VFR into IMC — a pilot trained only for Visual Flight Rules continuing into Instrument Meteorological Conditions (clouds, fog, reduced visibility) — is one of general aviation's most lethal accident categories. The fatality rate when this happens has stayed roughly 79-92% across decades. A 1954 University of Illinois study, repeatedly re-validated, found that non-instrument-rated pilots who entered cloud lost control of the aircraft within an average of 178 seconds — under three minutes from blue sky to spiral or stall. AOPA's Air Safety Institute reports that pilots flying in IMC are about 14× more likely to be involved in a fatal accident than those in VMC. In our slice the relevant columns are wx_cond_basic (VMC vs IMC) and flt_plan_filed (VFR / IFR / none); the canonical VFR-into-IMC pattern shows up as: pilot operating under VFR (no IFR plan) ends up in IMC weather, and the narr_cause field will often spell it out in plain language. This is the single highest-yield comparison in the dataset because both the data fields and the NTSB's own probable-cause text identify the pattern explicitly.

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: Probable-cause keyword taxonomy — what investigators actually say killed people
raw_evidence.content: Mining the 17,254 events with NTSB-written probable-cause text (98.5% coverage) for canonical accident-pattern keywords gives a fatality-weighted ranking that closely matches the GA-safety-literature consensus (det_06). Loss of control: 1,646 events / 51.2% fatal / 1,431 deaths. Aerodynamic stall: 1,420 / 49.9% fatal / 1,179 deaths. Engine failure: 3,876 events / 12.7% fatal / 732 deaths (very common but mostly survivable). Spatial disorientation: 298 events / 95.0% fatal / 558 deaths — the highest fatality rate of any high-volume pattern, almost always lethal. Controlled flight into terrain: 103 / 84.5% / 169. Structural failure / in-flight breakup: 97 / 85.6% / 168. Alcohol or drug impairment: 161 / 82.0% / 194. Stall-spin combined: 235 / 82.1% / 313. The pattern is consistent: rare events kill almost everyone they touch (disorientation, structural failure, alcohol), common events kill a minority (engine failure, landing accidents).

"spin": r"\bspin(s|ned|ning)?\b",
    "fuel_exhaustion": r"fuel exhaustion|exhausted (?:the )?fuel|out of fuel",

    "fuel_management": r"fuel (?:mis)?management|inadequate fuel",
    "engine_failure": r"engine failure|loss of engine power|partial loss of engine|engine malfunction",
    "vfr_into_imc": r"vfr (?:flight )?into (?:imc|instrument)|continued vfr flight into|continued visual flight into imc",
    "spatial_disorientation": r"spatial disorientation",
    "controlled_flight_into_terrain": r"controlled flight into terrain|cfit",
    "wire_strike": r"wire strike|struck (?:a |the )?wire|powerline",
    "bird_strike": r"bird strike|struck a bird",
    "icing": r"\bicing\b|airframe ice|carb(?:uretor)? ice",
    "go_around": r"go.?around",
    "runway_excursion": r"runway excursion|departed the runway|overran the runway|veered off the runway",
    "hard_landing": r"hard landing",
    "porpoise": r"porpois(e|ing)",
    "stall_spin": r"stall(\b.{0,20}\bspin)|stall/spin",
    "improper_decision": r"improper (?:decision|judgment)|inadequate decision",
    "pilot_inexperience": r"inexperience(?:d)?|insufficient (?:total )?experience",
    "alcohol_drugs": r"alcohol|impairment|drug",
    "midair_collision": r"mid.?air collision|midair collision",

    # Phases recovered from text — recovers what phase_flt_spec lost:
    "phase_takeoff": r"\b(takeoff|take.?off|initial climb)\b",

    "phase_approach": r"\bapproach\b",

# Roll one row per event (use first non-null cause text per event).
ev = df.groupby("ev_id").agg(
    cause=("cause_lc", "first"),
    fatal=("fatal", "any"),
    deaths=("inj_tot_f", "max"),
).reset_index()
total_events = ev.shape[0]
events_with_cause = ev[ev["cause"].str.len() > 0]
total_with_cause = events_with_cause.shape[0]
print(f"events_total: {total_events}")
print(f"events_with_cause_text: {total_with_cause}")
print(f"cause_text_coverage_pct: {total_with_cause / total_events * 100:.1f}")

rows = []
for name, pat in patterns.items():
    rx = re.compile(pat)
    hit = events_with_cause["cause"].str.contains(rx, regex=True)
    n = int(hit.sum())
    fatal_n = int(events_with_cause.loc[hit, "fatal"].sum())
    deaths = int(events_with_cause.loc[hit, "deaths"].sum())
    pct = (n / total_with_cause * 100) if total_with_cause else 0.0
    fpct = (fatal_n / n * 100) if n else 0.0
    rows.append({
        "pattern": name,
        "events": n,
        "events_pct": round(pct, 1),
        "fatal_events": fatal_n,
        "fatal_share_pct": round(fpct, 1),
        "deaths_sum": deaths,
    })

cause_tbl = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("events", ascending=False)
print(cause_tbl.to_string(index=False))

raw_evidence.label: VFR into IMC — the '178 seconds' problem
raw_evidence.content: VFR into IMC — a pilot trained only for Visual Flight Rules continuing into Instrument Meteorological Conditions (clouds, fog, reduced visibility) — is one of general aviation's most lethal accident categories. The fatality rate when this happens has stayed roughly 79-92% across decades. A 1954 University of Illinois study, repeatedly re-validated, found that non-instrument-rated pilots who entered cloud lost control of the aircraft within an average of 178 seconds — under three minutes from blue sky to spiral or stall. AOPA's Air Safety Institute reports that pilots flying in IMC are about 14× more likely to be involved in a fatal accident than those in VMC. In our slice the relevant columns are wx_cond_basic (VMC vs IMC) and flt_plan_filed (VFR / IFR / none); the canonical VFR-into-IMC pattern shows up as: pilot operating under VFR (no IFR plan) ends up in IMC weather, and the narr_cause field will often spell it out in plain language. This is the single highest-yield comparison in the dataset because both the data fields and the NTSB's own probable-cause text identify the pattern explicitly.

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: Probable-cause keyword taxonomy — what investigators actually say killed people
raw_evidence.content: Mining the 17,254 events with NTSB-written probable-cause text (98.5% coverage) for canonical accident-pattern keywords gives a fatality-weighted ranking that closely matches the GA-safety-literature consensus (det_06). Loss of control: 1,646 events / 51.2% fatal / 1,431 deaths. Aerodynamic stall: 1,420 / 49.9% fatal / 1,179 deaths. Engine failure: 3,876 events / 12.7% fatal / 732 deaths (very common but mostly survivable). Spatial disorientation: 298 events / 95.0% fatal / 558 deaths — the highest fatality rate of any high-volume pattern, almost always lethal. Controlled flight into terrain: 103 / 84.5% / 169. Structural failure / in-flight breakup: 97 / 85.6% / 168. Alcohol or drug impairment: 161 / 82.0% / 194. Stall-spin combined: 235 / 82.1% / 313. The pattern is consistent: rare events kill almost everyone they touch (disorientation, structural failure, alcohol), common events kill a minority (engine failure, landing accidents).

"spin": r"\bspin(s|ned|ning)?\b",
    "fuel_exhaustion": r"fuel exhaustion|exhausted (?:the )?fuel|out of fuel",
    "fuel_starvation": r"fuel starvation|starved of fuel",
    "fuel_management": r"fuel (?:mis)?management|inadequate fuel",
    "engine_failure": r"engine failure|loss of engine power|partial loss of engine|engine malfunction",
    "vfr_into_imc": r"vfr (?:flight )?into (?:imc|instrument)|continued vfr flight into|continued visual flight into imc",
    "spatial_disorientation": r"spatial disorientation",
    "controlled_flight_into_terrain": r"controlled flight into terrain|cfit",
    "wire_strike": r"wire strike|struck (?:a |the )?wire|powerline",
    "bird_strike": r"bird strike|struck a bird",
    "icing": r"\bicing\b|airframe ice|carb(?:uretor)? ice",
    "go_around": r"go.?around",
    "runway_excursion": r"runway excursion|departed the runway|overran the runway|veered off the runway",
    "hard_landing": r"hard landing",
    "porpoise": r"porpois(e|ing)",
    "stall_spin": r"stall(\b.{0,20}\bspin)|stall/spin",
    "improper_decision": r"improper (?:decision|judgment)|inadequate decision",
    "pilot_inexperience": r"inexperience(?:d)?|insufficient (?:total )?experience",
    "alcohol_drugs": r"alcohol|impairment|drug",
    "midair_collision": r"mid.?air collision|midair collision",
    "structural_failure": r"structural failure|in.?flight breakup|in.?flight break.?up",
    # Phases recovered from text — recovers what phase_flt_spec lost:
    "phase_takeoff": r"\b(takeoff|take.?off|initial climb)\b",
    "phase_landing": r"\b(landing|touchdown|flare)\b",
    "phase_approach": r"\bapproach\b",
    "phase_cruise": r"\bcruise\b",
    "phase_maneuvering": r"\bmaneuver(?:ing|ed)?\b",
    "phase_taxi": r"\btaxi(?:ing|ed)?\b",
}

# Roll one row per event (use first non-null cause text per event).
ev = df.groupby("ev_id").agg(
    cause=("cause_lc", "first"),
    fatal=("fatal", "any"),
    deaths=("inj_tot_f", "max"),
).reset_index()
total_events = ev.shape[0]
events_with_cause = ev[ev["cause"].str.len() > 0]
total_with_cause = events_with_cause.shape[0]
print(f"events_total: {total_events}")
print(f"events_with_cause_text: {total_with_cause}")
print(f"cause_text_coverage_pct: {total_with_cause / total_events * 100:.1f}")

rows = []
for name, pat in patterns.items():
    rx = re.compile(pat)
    hit = events_with_cause["cause"].str.contains(rx, regex=True)
    n = int(hit.sum())
    fatal_n = int(events_with_cause.loc[hit, "fatal"].sum())
    deaths = int(events_with_cause.loc[hit, "deaths"].sum())
    pct = (n / total_with_cause * 100) if total_with_cause else 0.0
    fpct = (fatal_n / n * 100) if n else 0.0
    rows.append({
        "pattern": name,
        "events": n,
        "events_pct": round(pct, 1),
        "fatal_events": fatal_n,
        "fatal_share_pct": round(fpct, 1),
        "deaths_sum": deaths,
    })

cause_tbl = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("events", ascending=False)
print(cause_tbl.to_string(index=False))

The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: VFR into IMC — the '178 seconds' problem
raw_evidence.content: VFR into IMC — a pilot trained only for Visual Flight Rules continuing into Instrument Meteorological Conditions (clouds, fog, reduced visibility) — is one of general aviation's most lethal accident categories. The fatality rate when this happens has stayed roughly 79-92% across decades. AOPA's Air Safety Institute reports that pilots flying in IMC are about 14× more likely to be involved in a fatal accident than those in VMC. In our slice the relevant columns are wx_cond_basic (VMC vs IMC) and flt_plan_filed (VFR / IFR / none); the canonical VFR-into-IMC pattern shows up as: pilot operating under VFR (no IFR plan) ends up in IMC weather, and the narr_cause field will often spell it out in plain language. This is the single highest-yield comparison in the dataset because both the data fields and the NTSB's own probable-cause text identify the pattern explicitly.

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: VFR into IMC — the '178 seconds' problem
raw_evidence.content: VFR into IMC — a pilot trained only for Visual Flight Rules continuing into Instrument Meteorological Conditions (clouds, fog, reduced visibility) — is one of general aviation's most lethal accident categories. The fatality rate when this happens has stayed roughly 79-92% across decades. A 1954 University of Illinois study, repeatedly re-validated, found that non-instrument-rated pilots who entered cloud lost control of the aircraft within an average of 178 seconds — under three minutes from blue sky to spiral or stall. AOPA's Air Safety Institute reports that pilots flying in IMC are about 14× more likely to be involved in a fatal accident than those in VMC. In our slice the relevant columns are wx_cond_basic (VMC vs IMC) and flt_plan_filed (VFR / IFR / none); the canonical VFR-into-IMC pattern shows up as: pilot operating under VFR (no IFR plan) ends up in IMC weather, and the narr_cause field will often spell it out in plain language. This is the single highest-yield comparison in the dataset because both the data fields and the NTSB's own probable-cause text identify the pattern explicitly.

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: VFR into IMC — the '178 seconds' problem
raw_evidence.content: VFR into IMC — a pilot trained only for Visual Flight Rules continuing into Instrument Meteorological Conditions (clouds, fog, reduced visibility) — is one of general aviation's most lethal accident categories. The fatality rate when this happens has stayed roughly 79-92% across decades. A 1954 University of Illinois study, repeatedly re-validated, found that non-instrument-rated pilots who entered cloud lost control of the aircraft within an average of 178 seconds — under three minutes from blue sky to spiral or stall. AOPA's Air Safety Institute reports that pilots flying in IMC are about 14× more likely to be involved in a fatal accident than those in VMC. In our slice the relevant columns are wx_cond_basic (VMC vs IMC) and flt_plan_filed (VFR / IFR / none); the canonical VFR-into-IMC pattern shows up as: pilot operating under VFR (no IFR plan) ends up in IMC weather, and the narr_cause field will often spell it out in plain language. This is the single highest-yield comparison in the dataset because both the data fields and the NTSB's own probable-cause text identify the pattern explicitly.

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

Spatial disorientation: 298 events / 95.0% fatal / 558 deaths — the highest fatality rate of any high-volume pattern, almost always lethal. Controlled flight into terrain: 103 / 84.5% / 169. Structural failure / in-flight breakup: 97 / 85.6% / 168. Alcohol or drug impairment: 161 / 82.0% / 194. Stall-spin combined: 235 / 82.1% / 313. The pattern is consistent: rare events kill almost everyone they touch (disorientation, structural failure, alcohol), common events kill a minority (engine failure, landing accidents).

raw_evidence.label: VFR into IMC — the '178 seconds' problem
raw_evidence.content: VFR into IMC — a pilot trained only for Visual Flight Rules continuing into Instrument Meteorological Conditions (clouds, fog, reduced visibility) — is one of general aviation's most lethal accident categories. The fatality rate when this happens has stayed roughly 79-92% across decades. A 1954 University of Illinois study, repeatedly re-validated, found that non-instrument-rated pilots who entered cloud lost control of the aircraft within an average of 178 seconds — under three minutes from blue sky to spiral or stall. AOPA's Air Safety Institute reports that pilots flying in IMC are about 14× more likely to be involved in a fatal accident than those in VMC. In our slice the relevant columns are wx_cond_basic (VMC vs IMC) and flt_plan_filed (VFR / IFR / none); the canonical VFR-into-IMC pattern shows up as: pilot operating under VFR (no IFR plan) ends up in IMC weather, and the narr_cause field will often spell it out in plain language. This is the single highest-yield comparison in the dataset because both the data fields and the NTSB's own probable-cause text identify the pattern explicitly.

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: VFR into IMC — the '178 seconds' problem
raw_evidence.content: VFR into IMC — a pilot trained only for Visual Flight Rules continuing into Instrument Meteorological Conditions (clouds, fog, reduced visibility) — is one of general aviation's most lethal accident categories. The fatality rate when this happens has stayed roughly 79-92% across decades. A 1954 University of Illinois study, repeatedly re-validated, found that non-instrument-rated pilots who entered cloud lost control of the aircraft within an average of 178 seconds — under three minutes from blue sky to spiral or stall. AOPA's Air Safety Institute reports that pilots flying in IMC are about 14× more likely to be involved in a fatal accident than those in VMC. In our slice the relevant columns are wx_cond_basic (VMC vs IMC) and flt_plan_filed (VFR / IFR / none); the canonical VFR-into-IMC pattern shows up as: pilot operating under VFR (no IFR plan) ends up in IMC weather, and the narr_cause field will often spell it out in plain language. This is the single highest-yield comparison in the dataset because both the data fields and the NTSB's own probable-cause text identify the pattern explicitly.

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

Engine failure: 3,876 events / 12.7% fatal / 732 deaths (very common but mostly survivable). Spatial disorientation: 298 events / 95.0% fatal / 558 deaths — the highest fatality rate of any high-volume pattern, almost always lethal. Controlled flight into terrain: 103 / 84.5% / 169. Structural failure / in-flight breakup: 97 / 85.6% / 168. Alcohol or drug impairment: 161 / 82.0% / 194. Stall-spin combined: 235 / 82.1% / 313. The pattern is consistent: rare events kill almost everyone they touch (disorientation, structural failure, alcohol), common events kill a minority (engine failure, landing accidents).

raw_evidence.label: Phase-of-flight recovered from text — maneuvering is 55% fatal
raw_evidence.content: Because phase_flt_spec is empty in this slice (a known limitation, ana_caveat_01), we recover phase signals from the narrative probable-cause text. The standout is maneuvering: just 815 mentions, but 55.1% of them are fatal — by far the most lethal phase, consistent with the long-recognized 'maneuvering at low altitude in a stall-friendly attitude' fatal-accident pattern. Cruise mentions are surprisingly rare (265, 1.5%) — most GA accidents happen near the ground, not in steady cruise flight.

raw_evidence.label: VFR into IMC — the '178 seconds' problem
raw_evidence.content: VFR into IMC — a pilot trained only for Visual Flight Rules continuing into Instrument Meteorological Conditions (clouds, fog, reduced visibility) — is one of general aviation's most lethal accident categories. The fatality rate when this happens has stayed roughly 79-92% across decades. A 1954 University of Illinois study, repeatedly re-validated, found that non-instrument-rated pilots who entered cloud lost control of the aircraft within an average of 178 seconds — under three minutes from blue sky to spiral or stall. AOPA's Air Safety Institute reports that pilots flying in IMC are about 14× more likely to be involved in a fatal accident than those in VMC. In our slice the relevant columns are wx_cond_basic (VMC vs IMC) and flt_plan_filed (VFR / IFR / none); the canonical VFR-into-IMC pattern shows up as: pilot operating under VFR (no IFR plan) ends up in IMC weather, and the narr_cause field will often spell it out in plain language. This is the single highest-yield comparison in the dataset because both the data fields and the NTSB's own probable-cause text identify the pattern explicitly.

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: VFR into IMC — the '178 seconds' problem
raw_evidence.content: VFR into IMC — a pilot trained only for Visual Flight Rules continuing into Instrument Meteorological Conditions (clouds, fog, reduced visibility) — is one of general aviation's most lethal accident categories. The fatality rate when this happens has stayed roughly 79-92% across decades. A 1954 University of Illinois study, repeatedly re-validated, found that non-instrument-rated pilots who entered cloud lost control of the aircraft within an average of 178 seconds — under three minutes from blue sky to spiral or stall. AOPA's Air Safety Institute reports that pilots flying in IMC are about 14× more likely to be involved in a fatal accident than those in VMC. In our slice the relevant columns are wx_cond_basic (VMC vs IMC) and flt_plan_filed (VFR / IFR / none); the canonical VFR-into-IMC pattern shows up as: pilot operating under VFR (no IFR plan) ends up in IMC weather, and the narr_cause field will often spell it out in plain language. This is the single highest-yield comparison in the dataset because both the data fields and the NTSB's own probable-cause text identify the pattern explicitly.

raw_evidence.label: Weather — IMC accidents are 4.2× as likely to be fatal as VMC
raw_evidence.content: When the weather at the time of the accident is logged as IMC (instrument meteorological conditions — clouds, low visibility), 64.9% of the resulting accidents are fatal. When it is logged as VMC, only 15.4% are. The ratio inside accidents is 4.2× — and the lower hours-denominator ratio in det_05 (14×) suggests the actual per-flight-hour danger of operating in IMC is even larger because the share of GA hours flown in IMC is small. IMC accidents are 4.1% of the slice (712 events) but contribute 462 of the 3,165 fatal events — 14.6% of all the deaths in the dataset, from 4% of the flying conditions.

ev = df.drop_duplicates("ev_id").copy()
ev_id_fatal = df.groupby("ev_id")["fatal"].any()
ev["any_fatal"] = ev["ev_id"].map(ev_id_fatal)

# --- ana_17: VMC vs IMC accident share + fatality share ---
print("=== ana_17 ===")
wx = ev.groupby(ev["wx_cond_basic"].fillna("UNK")).agg(
    events=("ev_id", "count"),
    fatal_events=("any_fatal", "sum"),
).reset_index().rename(columns={"wx_cond_basic": "wx"})
wx["share_of_events_pct"] = (wx.events / wx.events.sum() * 100).round(1)
wx["fatal_share_pct"] = (wx.fatal_events / wx.events * 100).round(1)
print(wx.to_string(index=False))

vmc_fatal = wx[wx.wx == "VMC"].fatal_share_pct.iat[0]

raw_evidence.label: VFR into IMC — the '178 seconds' problem
raw_evidence.content: VFR into IMC — a pilot trained only for Visual Flight Rules continuing into Instrument Meteorological Conditions (clouds, fog, reduced visibility) — is one of general aviation's most lethal accident categories. The fatality rate when this happens has stayed roughly 79-92% across decades. A 1954 University of Illinois study, repeatedly re-validated, found that non-instrument-rated pilots who entered cloud lost control of the aircraft within an average of 178 seconds — under three minutes from blue sky to spiral or stall. AOPA's Air Safety Institute reports that pilots flying in IMC are about 14× more likely to be involved in a fatal accident than those in VMC. In our slice the relevant columns are wx_cond_basic (VMC vs IMC) and flt_plan_filed (VFR / IFR / none); the canonical VFR-into-IMC pattern shows up as: pilot operating under VFR (no IFR plan) ends up in IMC weather, and the narr_cause field will often spell it out in plain language. This is the single highest-yield comparison in the dataset because both the data fields and the NTSB's own probable-cause text identify the pattern explicitly.

raw_evidence.label: VFR into IMC — 73% fatality rate, the dataset's deadliest single pattern
raw_evidence.content: Operationalizing det_05's canonical 'VFR pilot in IMC weather' pattern as wx_cond_basic = IMC AND flt_plan_filed != IFR (i.e. the pilot was not flying under instrument-flight rules and ended up in the clouds anyway), the dataset returns 336 events with a 72.9% fatal share — by far the deadliest single combination of structured-field conditions. The breakdown within IMC weather is even more striking: with no flight plan filed (NONE) the fatal share is 74.5%, with a filed VFR plan it is 66.7%, with a filed CVFR (controlled-VFR) it is 68.4%. Pilots who did file IFR and were in IMC still had a 58.2% fatal share — instrument flying in IMC is not safe in absolute terms, it is just two orders of magnitude safer than VFR flying in IMC per flight hour.
raw_evidence.code:
print(f"VMC fatal_share: {vmc_fatal}%")
print(f"IMC fatal_share: {imc_fatal}%")
print(f"IMC vs VMC ratio: {imc_fatal / vmc_fatal:.1f}x")

# --- ana_18: VFR-into-IMC — IMC weather with non-IFR flight plan ---
print("=== ana_18 ===")
# Define the canonical pattern from det_05: wx = IMC, flight plan != IFR (NONE / VFR / CVFR / MVFR / NaN / UNK)
def is_vfr_into_imc(row) -> bool:
    if pd.isna(row.wx_cond_basic) or row.wx_cond_basic != "IMC":
        return False
    fp = row.flt_plan_filed
    if pd.isna(fp):
        return True  # absence of plan in IMC counts
    return fp in {"NONE", "VFR", "CVFR", "MVFR", "UNK"}


ev["vfr_into_imc"] = ev.apply(is_vfr_into_imc, axis=1)
v = ev.groupby("vfr_into_imc").agg(events=("ev_id", "count"), fatal_events=("any_fatal", "sum")).reset_index()
v["fatal_share_pct"] = (v.fatal_events / v.events * 100).round(1)
print(v.to_string(index=False))

# Sub-table for a 2x2 chart: weather × flight-plan-class
ev["fp_class"] = ev.flt_plan_filed.where(
    ev.flt_plan_filed.isin(["IFR", "VFR", "CVFR", "NONE", "MVFR", "VFIF"]),
    "OTHER",
).fillna("MISSING")
ev["wx_class"] = ev.wx_cond_basic.where(ev.wx_cond_basic.isin(["VMC", "IMC"]), "UNK").fillna("UNK")
matrix = ev.groupby(["wx_class", "fp_class"]).agg(
    events=("ev_id", "count"),

         True     336           245             72.9
wx_class fp_class  events  fatal_events  fatal_share_pct

     IMC      IFR     371           216             58.2
     IMC     NONE     275           205             74.5
     IMC      VFR      27            18             66.7

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.content: 90% of GA Part-91 accidents happen in daylight (15,809 events), with a fatal share of 16.2%. Night accidents are 6.4% of events (1,119 once Night/Night-dark/Night-bright are combined) but their fatal share is 37.4% — 2.3× the daylight rate. The dark-night sub-bucket (NDRK, no moon / heavy cloud cover) is the worst at 55.6% fatal share over 313 events. Dawn and dusk twilight are essentially equal to daylight in fatality at 17.7%, which suggests it is the absence of visual reference, not low ambient light per se, that makes the difference.

raw_evidence.label: Day vs night — night fatal share is 2.3× day, dark-night is 3.4×
raw_evidence.content: 90% of GA Part-91 accidents happen in daylight (15,809 events), with a fatal share of 16.2%. Night accidents are 6.4% of events (1,119 once Night/Night-dark/Night-bright are combined) but their fatal share is 37.4% — 2.3× the daylight rate. The dark-night sub-bucket (NDRK, no moon / heavy cloud cover) is the worst at 55.6% fatal share over 313 events. Dawn and dusk twilight are essentially equal to daylight in fatality at 17.7%, which suggests it is the absence of visual reference, not low ambient light per se, that makes the difference.

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: Alaska — the per-flight-hour outlier
raw_evidence.content: Alaska is a special case in U.S. general aviation. For much of the state, aviation is not a hobby but transportation infrastructure: villages are reachable only by floatplane, ski-equipped Cessna, or chartered Piper Navajo. The state's accident rate reflects this. A 2004-2008 analysis put Alaska's GA accident rate at 13.59 per 100,000 flight hours versus a national 5.85 — more than double. ProPublica reported in 2021 that Alaska accounts for a growing share of the country's deadly aviation crashes. The drivers are structural: rapidly changing weather around mountains and coastal fjords, large stretches of uncontrolled airspace without ground-based weather or radar coverage, short and unpaved backcountry strips, and what Alaskan safety researchers call 'bush syndrome' — pilots accepting unnecessary risk to complete a flight because the alternative is leaving a customer or a load stranded for days. In our dataset, ev_state = 'AK' will be a meaningful slice, and joining it with phase_flt_spec, light_cond, and wx_cond_basic will probably show a heavier weighting toward maneuvering / approach / IMC accidents than the lower-48 average.

raw_evidence.label: Top states by accidents — CA, TX, FL lead; Alaska is the surprise
raw_evidence.content: California (1,575), Texas (1,513) and Florida (1,385) lead the absolute counts — unsurprising given they are the three largest states by both population and registered GA aircraft. Alaska is the fourth-most-accident-prone state with 1,016 events, despite having less than 1% of U.S. population. Per-capita that puts Alaska at roughly 7-8× the lower-48 rate, consistent with det_07's hours-based 2× figure (Alaska also flies vastly more per capita). The fatal-share split is the interesting twist: see ana_14.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_14: Events and fatalities by state, top 15 ---
print("=== ana_14 ===")
ev = df.drop_duplicates("ev_id")
fatal_by_ev = df.groupby("ev_id")["inj_tot_f"].max().reset_index()
ev = ev.merge(fatal_by_ev, on="ev_id", suffixes=("", "_x"))
state = ev.groupby("ev_state").agg(
    events=("ev_id", "count"),
    fatal_events=("inj_tot_f", lambda x: (x > 0).sum()),
    deaths=("inj_tot_f", "sum"),
).reset_index().sort_values("events", ascending=False)
total_ev = ev.shape[0]
state["events_share_pct"] = (state.events / total_ev * 100).round(1)

raw_evidence.label: Alaska — the per-flight-hour outlier
raw_evidence.content: Alaska is a special case in U.S. general aviation. For much of the state, aviation is not a hobby but transportation infrastructure: villages are reachable only by floatplane, ski-equipped Cessna, or chartered Piper Navajo. The state's accident rate reflects this. A 2004-2008 analysis put Alaska's GA accident rate at 13.59 per 100,000 flight hours versus a national 5.85 — more than double. ProPublica reported in 2021 that Alaska accounts for a growing share of the country's deadly aviation crashes. The drivers are structural: rapidly changing weather around mountains and coastal fjords, large stretches of uncontrolled airspace without ground-based weather or radar coverage, short and unpaved backcountry strips, and what Alaskan safety researchers call 'bush syndrome' — pilots accepting unnecessary risk to complete a flight because the alternative is leaving a customer or a load stranded for days. In our dataset, ev_state = 'AK' will be a meaningful slice, and joining it with phase_flt_spec, light_cond, and wx_cond_basic will probably show a heavier weighting toward maneuvering / approach / IMC accidents than the lower-48 average.
