raw_evidence.label: Top states by accidents — CA, TX, FL lead; Alaska is the surprise
raw_evidence.content: California (1,575), Texas (1,513) and Florida (1,385) lead the absolute counts — unsurprising given they are the three largest states by both population and registered GA aircraft. Alaska is the fourth-most-accident-prone state with 1,016 events, despite having less than 1% of U.S. population. Per-capita that puts Alaska at roughly 7-8× the lower-48 rate, consistent with det_07's hours-based 2× figure (Alaska also flies vastly more per capita). The fatal-share split is the interesting twist: see ana_14.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_14: Events and fatalities by state, top 15 ---
print("=== ana_14 ===")
ev = df.drop_duplicates("ev_id")
fatal_by_ev = df.groupby("ev_id")["inj_tot_f"].max().reset_index()
ev = ev.merge(fatal_by_ev, on="ev_id", suffixes=("", "_x"))
state = ev.groupby("ev_state").agg(
    events=("ev_id", "count"),
    fatal_events=("inj_tot_f", lambda x: (x > 0).sum()),
    deaths=("inj_tot_f", "sum"),
).reset_index().sort_values("events", ascending=False)
total_ev = ev.shape[0]
state["events_share_pct"] = (state.events / total_ev * 100).round(1)

raw_evidence.label: The Alaska paradox — many accidents, fewer fatal ones
raw_evidence.content: Alaska has 5.8% of all GA Part-91 accidents but only 9.6% of those accidents are fatal — about half the lower-48 rate of 18.2%. Said another way: the Alaska GA accident rate per flight hour is roughly 2× the U.S. average, but the per-crash fatality rate is roughly half. The likeliest explanation is that a lot of Alaskan GA flying is short-range, low-altitude, low-speed bush operation onto unimproved strips, ridges, sandbars and water; those crashes mangle airframes but do not kill the people in them at the rate that a wings-level cruise impact does. Detective det_07 lays out the structural reasons (rapid weather, unpaved strips, 'bush syndrome'); the data refines them to: yes, more accidents, but more survivable ones.
raw_evidence.code:
print(state.head(15).to_string(index=False))

# --- ana_15: Alaska focused split ---
print("=== ana_15 ===")
ak = state[state.ev_state == "AK"].iloc[0]
print(f"AK events: {ak.events}  ({ak.events_share_pct}% of all)")
print(f"AK deaths: {int(ak.deaths)}")
print(f"AK fatal_share_pct: {ak.fatal_share_pct}")
# compare AK fatal share with rest-of-US fatal share
rest = ev[ev.ev_state != "AK"]
rest_events = rest.shape[0]

raw_evidence.label: Alaska — the per-flight-hour outlier
raw_evidence.content: Alaska is a special case in U.S. general aviation. For much of the state, aviation is not a hobby but transportation infrastructure: villages are reachable only by floatplane, ski-equipped Cessna, or chartered Piper Navajo. The state's accident rate reflects this. A 2004-2008 analysis put Alaska's GA accident rate at 13.59 per 100,000 flight hours versus a national 5.85 — more than double. ProPublica reported in 2021 that Alaska accounts for a growing share of the country's deadly aviation crashes. The drivers are structural: rapidly changing weather around mountains and coastal fjords, large stretches of uncontrolled airspace without ground-based weather or radar coverage, short and unpaved backcountry strips, and what Alaskan safety researchers call 'bush syndrome' — pilots accepting unnecessary risk to complete a flight because the alternative is leaving a customer or a load stranded for days. In our dataset, ev_state = 'AK' will be a meaningful slice, and joining it with phase_flt_spec, light_cond, and wx_cond_basic will probably show a heavier weighting toward maneuvering / approach / IMC accidents than the lower-48 average.

raw_evidence.label: The homebuilt-aircraft fatality premium
raw_evidence.content: Experimental / amateur-built (E/A-B) aircraft — homebuilt kit planes like the Van's RV series, the Lancair Legacy, the Glasair, the Sonex — have a measurably worse fatal accident profile than factory-certificated GA aircraft. The 2012 NTSB safety study on E/A-B aircraft (NTSB/SS-12/01) found the E/A-B fatal accident rate over 2001-2010 was roughly four times higher than non-E/A-B aircraft. More recent industry analyses put the overall accident rate for homebuilts at about 2.5× the GA average, and roughly 4× higher than common type-certificated trainers like the Cessna 172, with equipment-related fatal accidents appearing at roughly twice the rate of certificated airplanes. The data field that flags this in our slice is homebuilt = 'Y'. Because there are 17,712 rows and homebuilts make up roughly 10-15% of the GA fleet by some measures, even a moderately elevated fatality rate among homebuilts shows up clearly in this dataset — the Analyst should look at fatal-share by homebuilt status as one of the cleanest 'big number' comparisons available.

raw_evidence.label: Cessna and Piper dominate the fleet — and the accident record
raw_evidence.content: The U.S. GA fleet is heavily skewed toward a small number of long-lived single-engine piston designs. By cumulative NTSB record, more than half of all aviation accidents in the database involve Cessna (~25,865 crashes historically), Piper (~14,105), or Beech (~5,098) aircraft. The Cessna 172 Skyhawk is the most-built airplane in history (over 44,000 produced since 1956) and serves as the default trainer for most American flight schools. Per-hour, its fatal accident rate is actually low — historical estimates from AOPA put the 172 at ~0.56 fatal accidents per 100,000 flight hours against a fleet average of 1.2-1.4 — but in absolute counts it appears constantly because there are so many of them flying. The Analyst should therefore distinguish between two questions: 'which airplane shows up the most often?' (Cessna 172, by far) and 'which airplane is most dangerous per hour?' (a very different question, harder to answer without an exposure denominator we don't have in this slice). The naming is also a known data-quality wrinkle: acft_make is a free-text field, so 'CESSNA', 'Cessna', and 'CESSNA AIRCRAFT' may all appear — the Analyst will need to normalize.

raw_evidence.label: Top manufacturer brands — Cessna 27%, Piper 17%, Beech 6%
raw_evidence.content: After normalizing the free-text acft_make column into canonical brand buckets, the three biggest manufacturers account for half of all GA Part 91 accidents in the dataset: Cessna 27.3% (4,781 events), Piper 16.8% (2,936) and Beech 6.3% (1,104). The next tier — Robinson (helicopters), Bell (helicopters), Cirrus, Mooney — each contribute 2-3%. Crucially, the per-brand fatal-share among accidents tells a different story than count: Beech and Cirrus aircraft, which include high-performance singles like the Bonanza and the SR22, each have fatal shares near 27% — well above Cessna's 13.8% — consistent with their faster cruise speeds and the energy-management challenges that come with them. Van's homebuilt kit planes (RV series) come in at 28.8% fatal share, again above the certificated-Cessna baseline.
raw_evidence.code:
df["brand"] = df["acft_make"].apply(brand_of)


# --- ana_08: Top manufacturer brands by accident count ---
print("=== ana_08 ===")
b = df.groupby("brand").agg(events=("ev_id", "nunique"), fatal_events=("fatal", "sum")).reset_index()
b["fatal_share_pct"] = (b.fatal_events / b.events * 100).round(1)
b = b.sort_values("events", ascending=False)
total_ev = df.ev_id.nunique()
b["share_of_all_pct"] = (b.events / total_ev * 100).round(1)

More recent industry analyses put the overall accident rate for homebuilts at about 2.5× the GA average, and roughly 4× higher than common type-certificated trainers like the Cessna 172, with equipment-related fatal accidents appearing at roughly twice the rate of certificated airplanes. The data field that flags this in our slice is homebuilt = 'Y'. Because there are 17,712 rows and homebuilts make up roughly 10-15% of the GA fleet by some measures, even a moderately elevated fatality rate among homebuilts shows up clearly in this dataset — the Analyst should look at fatal-share by homebuilt status as one of the cleanest 'big number' comparisons available.

raw_evidence.label: Cessna and Piper dominate the fleet — and the accident record
raw_evidence.content: The U.S. GA fleet is heavily skewed toward a small number of long-lived single-engine piston designs. By cumulative NTSB record, more than half of all aviation accidents in the database involve Cessna (~25,865 crashes historically), Piper (~14,105), or Beech (~5,098) aircraft. The Cessna 172 Skyhawk is the most-built airplane in history (over 44,000 produced since 1956) and serves as the default trainer for most American flight schools. Per-hour, its fatal accident rate is actually low — historical estimates from AOPA put the 172 at ~0.56 fatal accidents per 100,000 flight hours against a fleet average of 1.2-1.4 — but in absolute counts it appears constantly because there are so many of them flying. The Analyst should therefore distinguish between two questions: 'which airplane shows up the most often?' (Cessna 172, by far) and 'which airplane is most dangerous per hour?' (a very different question, harder to answer without an exposure denominator we don't have in this slice). The naming is also a known data-quality wrinkle: acft_make is a free-text field, so 'CESSNA', 'Cessna', and 'CESSNA AIRCRAFT' may all appear — the Analyst will need to normalize.

raw_evidence.label: Top manufacturer brands — Cessna 27%, Piper 17%, Beech 6%
raw_evidence.content: After normalizing the free-text acft_make column into canonical brand buckets, the three biggest manufacturers account for half of all GA Part 91 accidents in the dataset: Cessna 27.3% (4,781 events), Piper 16.8% (2,936) and Beech 6.3% (1,104). The next tier — Robinson (helicopters), Bell (helicopters), Cirrus, Mooney — each contribute 2-3%. Crucially, the per-brand fatal-share among accidents tells a different story than count: Beech and Cirrus aircraft, which include high-performance singles like the Bonanza and the SR22, each have fatal shares near 27% — well above Cessna's 13.8% — consistent with their faster cruise speeds and the energy-management challenges that come with them. Van's homebuilt kit planes (RV series) come in at 28.8% fatal share, again above the certificated-Cessna baseline.

raw_evidence.label: Homebuilt premium — 22% fatal share vs 17% for factory aircraft
raw_evidence.content: Among the 17,543 distinct events with a known homebuilt status, 2,745 (15.6%) were homebuilt and 14,798 (84.4%) were factory-certificated. The fatal share inside accidents is meaningfully higher for homebuilts: 22.2% versus 17.3% — a 1.28× ratio. This is smaller than the 4× per-flight-hour ratio the NTSB safety study (det_04) reports, but the two numbers measure different things: the NTSB's 4× ratio compares fatal accidents per 100,000 flight hours and includes the higher accident exposure of homebuilts; the 1.28× ratio here is fatal-share-conditional-on-having-an-accident, which is closer to a 'severity per crash' figure. The Editor should be explicit that the per-hour premium and the per-accident severity premium are different statistics. Even the within-accidents-severity premium of 1.28× translates to ~138 extra fatal events over the 15-year window if homebuilts had crashed at the factory rate.
raw_evidence.code:
events=("ev_id", "nunique"),
    fatal_events=("fatal", "sum"),
).reset_index().rename(columns={"homebuilt": "homebuilt_flag"})
hb["fatal_share_pct"] = (hb.fatal_events / hb.events * 100).round(1)
print(hb.to_string(index=False))
# Detective det_04 claims roughly 4x higher fatal rate for E/A-B versus certificated.
# We can't compute per-100k-hour rate without exposure denominator, but we can compare fatal-share within accidents.
hb_y = hb[hb.homebuilt_flag == "Y"].fatal_share_pct.iat[0]
hb_n = hb[hb.homebuilt_flag == "N"].fatal_share_pct.iat[0]
print(f"homebuilt_fatal_share_pct: {hb_y}")
print(f"factory_fatal_share_pct: {hb_n}")
print(f"ratio_homebuilt_over_factory: {hb_y / hb_n:.2f}x")

raw_evidence.label: Cessna and Piper dominate the fleet — and the accident record
raw_evidence.content: The U.S. GA fleet is heavily skewed toward a small number of long-lived single-engine piston designs. By cumulative NTSB record, more than half of all aviation accidents in the database involve Cessna (~25,865 crashes historically), Piper (~14,105), or Beech (~5,098) aircraft. The Cessna 172 Skyhawk is the most-built airplane in history (over 44,000 produced since 1956) and serves as the default trainer for most American flight schools. Per-hour, its fatal accident rate is actually low — historical estimates from AOPA put the 172 at ~0.56 fatal accidents per 100,000 flight hours against a fleet average of 1.2-1.4 — but in absolute counts it appears constantly because there are so many of them flying. The Analyst should therefore distinguish between two questions: 'which airplane shows up the most often?' (Cessna 172, by far) and 'which airplane is most dangerous per hour?' (a very different question, harder to answer without an exposure denominator we don't have in this slice). The naming is also a known data-quality wrinkle: acft_make is a free-text field, so 'CESSNA', 'Cessna', and 'CESSNA AIRCRAFT' may all appear — the Analyst will need to normalize.

raw_evidence.label: The homebuilt-aircraft fatality premium
raw_evidence.content: Experimental / amateur-built (E/A-B) aircraft — homebuilt kit planes like the Van's RV series, the Lancair Legacy, the Glasair, the Sonex — have a measurably worse fatal accident profile than factory-certificated GA aircraft. The 2012 NTSB safety study on E/A-B aircraft (NTSB/SS-12/01) found the E/A-B fatal accident rate over 2001-2010 was roughly four times higher than non-E/A-B aircraft. More recent industry analyses put the overall accident rate for homebuilts at about 2.5× the GA average, and roughly 4× higher than common type-certificated trainers like the Cessna 172, with equipment-related fatal accidents appearing at roughly twice the rate of certificated airplanes. The data field that flags this in our slice is homebuilt = 'Y'. Because there are 17,712 rows and homebuilts make up roughly 10-15% of the GA fleet by some measures, even a moderately elevated fatality rate among homebuilts shows up clearly in this dataset — the Analyst should look at fatal-share by homebuilt status as one of the cleanest 'big number' comparisons available.

raw_evidence.label: Cessna and Piper dominate the fleet — and the accident record
raw_evidence.content: The U.S. GA fleet is heavily skewed toward a small number of long-lived single-engine piston designs. By cumulative NTSB record, more than half of all aviation accidents in the database involve Cessna (~25,865 crashes historically), Piper (~14,105), or Beech (~5,098) aircraft. The Cessna 172 Skyhawk is the most-built airplane in history (over 44,000 produced since 1956) and serves as the default trainer for most American flight schools. Per-hour, its fatal accident rate is actually low — historical estimates from AOPA put the 172 at ~0.56 fatal accidents per 100,000 flight hours against a fleet average of 1.2-1.4 — but in absolute counts it appears constantly because there are so many of them flying. The Analyst should therefore distinguish between two questions: 'which airplane shows up the most often?' (Cessna 172, by far) and 'which airplane is most dangerous per hour?' (a very different question, harder to answer without an exposure denominator we don't have in this slice). The naming is also a known data-quality wrinkle: acft_make is a free-text field, so 'CESSNA', 'Cessna', and 'CESSNA AIRCRAFT' may all appear — the Analyst will need to normalize.

raw_evidence.label: Homebuilt premium — 22% fatal share vs 17% for factory aircraft
raw_evidence.content: Among the 17,543 distinct events with a known homebuilt status, 2,745 (15.6%) were homebuilt and 14,798 (84.4%) were factory-certificated. The fatal share inside accidents is meaningfully higher for homebuilts: 22.2% versus 17.3% — a 1.28× ratio. This is smaller than the 4× per-flight-hour ratio the NTSB safety study (det_04) reports, but the two numbers measure different things: the NTSB's 4× ratio compares fatal accidents per 100,000 flight hours and includes the higher accident exposure of homebuilts; the 1.28× ratio here is fatal-share-conditional-on-having-an-accident, which is closer to a 'severity per crash' figure. The Editor should be explicit that the per-hour premium and the per-accident severity premium are different statistics. Even the within-accidents-severity premium of 1.28× translates to ~138 extra fatal events over the 15-year window if homebuilts had crashed at the factory rate.
raw_evidence.code:
events=("ev_id", "nunique"),
    fatal_events=("fatal", "sum"),
).reset_index().rename(columns={"homebuilt": "homebuilt_flag"})
hb["fatal_share_pct"] = (hb.fatal_events / hb.events * 100).round(1)
print(hb.to_string(index=False))
# Detective det_04 claims roughly 4x higher fatal rate for E/A-B versus certificated.
# We can't compute per-100k-hour rate without exposure denominator, but we can compare fatal-share within accidents.
hb_y = hb[hb.homebuilt_flag == "Y"].fatal_share_pct.iat[0]
hb_n = hb[hb.homebuilt_flag == "N"].fatal_share_pct.iat[0]
print(f"homebuilt_fatal_share_pct: {hb_y}")
print(f"factory_fatal_share_pct: {hb_n}")
print(f"ratio_homebuilt_over_factory: {hb_y / hb_n:.2f}x")
raw_evidence.output:
homebuilt_flag  aircraft_rows  events  fatal_events  fatal_share_pct
             N          14954   14798          2556             17.3
             Y           2758    2745           609             22.2
ratio_homebuilt_over_factory: 1.28x

raw_evidence.label: The fleet that won't quit
raw_evidence.editorial_notes: The 39-year median fleet age is the surprising statistic for general readers. Designer should make this the visual hook. The homebuilt 1.28× vs det_04's 4× distinction MUST be in the prose — it is a common misconception correction. Cessna/Piper/Beech share-of-accidents can be a sidebar stat callout.

raw_evidence.label: Homebuilt-premium guess-first reveal
raw_evidence.brief: A one-question guess-first interaction sitting above the edt_08 inset chart. The reader picks 1×/2×/4×/8× as the homebuilt fatality premium, then sees the inset chart with the 1.28× per-accident vs 4× per-hour distinction explicitly called out. The interaction is what makes the caveat memorable — passive readers usually miss the per-hour-vs-per-accident gotcha in the prose.

raw_evidence.label: The homebuilt-aircraft fatality premium
raw_evidence.content: Experimental / amateur-built (E/A-B) aircraft — homebuilt kit planes like the Van's RV series, the Lancair Legacy, the Glasair, the Sonex — have a measurably worse fatal accident profile than factory-certificated GA aircraft. The data field that flags this in our slice is homebuilt = 'Y'. raw_evidence.label: Cessna and Piper dominate the fleet — and the accident record
raw_evidence.content: The U.S. GA fleet is heavily skewed toward a small number of long-lived single-engine piston designs. By cumulative NTSB record, more than half of all aviation accidents in the database involve Cessna (~25,865 crashes historically), Piper (~14,105), or Beech (~5,098) aircraft. The Cessna 172 Skyhawk is the most-built airplane in history (over 44,000 produced since 1956) and serves as the default trainer for most American flight schools. Per-hour, its fatal accident rate is actually low — historical estimates from AOPA put the 172 at ~0.56 fatal accidents per 100,000 flight hours against a fleet average of 1.2-1.4 — but in absolute counts it appears constantly because there are so many of them flying. The Analyst should therefore distinguish between two questions: 'which airplane shows up the most often?' (Cessna 172, by far) and 'which airplane is most dangerous per hour?' (a very different question, harder to answer without an exposure denominator we don't have in this slice). raw_evidence.label: Homebuilt premium — 22% fatal share vs 17% for factory aircraft
raw_evidence.content: Among the 17,543 distinct events with a known homebuilt status, 2,745 (15.6%) were homebuilt and 14,798 (84.4%) were factory-certificated. The fatal share inside accidents is meaningfully higher for homebuilts: 22.2% versus 17.3% — a 1.28× ratio. This is smaller than the 4× per-flight-hour ratio the NTSB safety study (det_04) reports, but the two numbers measure different things: the NTSB's 4× ratio compares fatal accidents per 100,000 flight hours and includes the higher accident exposure of homebuilts; the 1.28× ratio here is fatal-share-conditional-on-having-an-accident, which is closer to a 'severity per crash' figure. The Editor should be explicit that the per-hour premium and the per-accident severity premium are different statistics. Even the within-accidents-severity premium of 1.28× translates to ~138 extra fatal events over the 15-year window if homebuilts had crashed at the factory rate.
raw_evidence.code:
events=("ev_id", "nunique"),
    fatal_events=("fatal", "sum"),
).reset_index().rename(columns={"homebuilt": "homebuilt_flag"})
hb["fatal_share_pct"] = (hb.fatal_events / hb.events * 100).round(1)
print(hb.to_string(index=False))
# Detective det_04 claims roughly 4x higher fatal rate for E/A-B versus certificated.
# We can't compute per-100k-hour rate without exposure denominator, but we can compare fatal-share within accidents.
hb_y = hb[hb.homebuilt_flag == "Y"].fatal_share_pct.iat[0]
hb_n = hb[hb.homebuilt_flag == "N"].fatal_share_pct.iat[0]
print(f"homebuilt_fatal_share_pct: {hb_y}")
print(f"factory_fatal_share_pct: {hb_n}")
print(f"ratio_homebuilt_over_factory: {hb_y / hb_n:.2f}x")
raw_evidence.output:
homebuilt_flag  aircraft_rows  events  fatal_events  fatal_share_pct
             N          14954   14798          2556             17.3
             Y           2758    2745           609             22.2
ratio_homebuilt_over_factory: 1.28x

This is smaller than the 4× per-flight-hour ratio the NTSB safety study (det_04) reports, but the two numbers measure different things: the NTSB's 4× ratio compares fatal accidents per 100,000 flight hours and includes the higher accident exposure of homebuilts; the 1.28× ratio here is fatal-share-conditional-on-having-an-accident, which is closer to a 'severity per crash' figure. The Editor should be explicit that the per-hour premium and the per-accident severity premium are different statistics. raw_evidence.label: The homebuilt-aircraft fatality premium
raw_evidence.content: Experimental / amateur-built (E/A-B) aircraft — homebuilt kit planes like the Van's RV series, the Lancair Legacy, the Glasair, the Sonex — have a measurably worse fatal accident profile than factory-certificated GA aircraft. The 2012 NTSB safety study on E/A-B aircraft (NTSB/SS-12/01) found the E/A-B fatal accident rate over 2001-2010 was roughly four times higher than non-E/A-B aircraft. More recent industry analyses put the overall accident rate for homebuilts at about 2.5× the GA average, and roughly 4× higher than common type-certificated trainers like the Cessna 172, with equipment-related fatal accidents appearing at roughly twice the rate of certificated airplanes. The data field that flags this in our slice is homebuilt = 'Y'. Because there are 17,712 rows and homebuilts make up roughly 10-15% of the GA fleet by some measures, even a moderately elevated fatality rate among homebuilts shows up clearly in this dataset — the Analyst should look at fatal-share by homebuilt status as one of the cleanest 'big number' comparisons available.

raw_evidence.label: Cessna and Piper dominate the fleet — and the accident record
raw_evidence.content: The U.S. GA fleet is heavily skewed toward a small number of long-lived single-engine piston designs. By cumulative NTSB record, more than half of all aviation accidents in the database involve Cessna (~25,865 crashes historically), Piper (~14,105), or Beech (~5,098) aircraft. The Cessna 172 Skyhawk is the most-built airplane in history (over 44,000 produced since 1956) and serves as the default trainer for most American flight schools. Per-hour, its fatal accident rate is actually low — historical estimates from AOPA put the 172 at ~0.56 fatal accidents per 100,000 flight hours against a fleet average of 1.2-1.4 — but in absolute counts it appears constantly because there are so many of them flying. The Analyst should therefore distinguish between two questions: 'which airplane shows up the most often?' (Cessna 172, by far) and 'which airplane is most dangerous per hour?' (a very different question, harder to answer without an exposure denominator we don't have in this slice). The naming is also a known data-quality wrinkle: acft_make is a free-text field, so 'CESSNA', 'Cessna', and 'CESSNA AIRCRAFT' may all appear — the Analyst will need to normalize.

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: Why this story matters — the gap between flying-as-airline-passenger and flying-as-private-pilot
raw_evidence.content: U.S. commercial aviation is one of the safest forms of transportation ever engineered: the airlines have flown for years on end without a passenger fatality in the U.S. General aviation is a different story. A private pilot in a Cessna 172 is operating in a regulatory regime, training environment, weather-decision context, and maintenance economy that is meaningfully closer to driving a car than to riding on Delta. The gap matters for two reasons. First, it shapes public perception: small-plane crashes generate disproportionate local-news coverage relative to airline accidents because they are common enough to be regular and rare enough to still be newsworthy. Second, the regulatory and educational levers that fixed airline safety in the 1990s and 2000s (crew resource management, sophisticated simulator training, two-pilot crews, mandatory route planning) only partly map onto single-pilot light-aircraft operations. So the story this dataset can tell — what kills private pilots, where, in what airplanes, in what weather — is also the story of a safety problem that the easy fixes have already been applied to and which remains stubbornly resistant to the next wave of fixes.

raw_evidence.label: Phase-of-flight recovered from text — maneuvering is 55% fatal
raw_evidence.content: Because phase_flt_spec is empty in this slice (a known limitation, ana_caveat_01), we recover phase signals from the narrative probable-cause text. Landing-phase mentions are by far the most common (6,940 events, 40.2% of cause-text coverage) but only 4.4% fatal — most landing accidents are low-speed and survivable. Takeoff mentions: 2,628 events, 17.9% fatal. Approach: 1,149, 21.3% fatal. The standout is maneuvering: just 815 mentions, but 55.1% of them are fatal — by far the most lethal phase, consistent with the long-recognized 'maneuvering at low altitude in a stall-friendly attitude' fatal-accident pattern. Cruise mentions are surprisingly rare (265, 1.5%) — most GA accidents happen near the ground, not in steady cruise flight.

raw_evidence.label: Probable-cause keyword taxonomy — what investigators actually say killed people
raw_evidence.content: Mining the 17,254 events with NTSB-written probable-cause text (98.5% coverage) for canonical accident-pattern keywords gives a fatality-weighted ranking that closely matches the GA-safety-literature consensus (det_06). Loss of control: 1,646 events / 51.2% fatal / 1,431 deaths. Aerodynamic stall: 1,420 / 49.9% fatal / 1,179 deaths. Engine failure: 3,876 events / 12.7% fatal / 732 deaths (very common but mostly survivable). Spatial disorientation: 298 events / 95.0% fatal / 558 deaths — the highest fatality rate of any high-volume pattern, almost always lethal. Controlled flight into terrain: 103 / 84.5% / 169. Structural failure / in-flight breakup: 97 / 85.6% / 168. Alcohol or drug impairment: 161 / 82.0% / 194. Stall-spin combined: 235 / 82.1% / 313. The pattern is consistent: rare events kill almost everyone they touch (disorientation, structural failure, alcohol), common events kill a minority (engine failure, landing accidents).

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: Why this story matters — the gap between flying-as-airline-passenger and flying-as-private-pilot
raw_evidence.content: U.S. commercial aviation is one of the safest forms of transportation ever engineered: the airlines have flown for years on end without a passenger fatality in the U.S. General aviation is a different story. A private pilot in a Cessna 172 is operating in a regulatory regime, training environment, weather-decision context, and maintenance economy that is meaningfully closer to driving a car than to riding on Delta. The gap matters for two reasons. First, it shapes public perception: small-plane crashes generate disproportionate local-news coverage relative to airline accidents because they are common enough to be regular and rare enough to still be newsworthy. Second, the regulatory and educational levers that fixed airline safety in the 1990s and 2000s (crew resource management, sophisticated simulator training, two-pilot crews, mandatory route planning) only partly map onto single-pilot light-aircraft operations. So the story this dataset can tell — what kills private pilots, where, in what airplanes, in what weather — is also the story of a safety problem that the easy fixes have already been applied to and which remains stubbornly resistant to the next wave of fixes.

raw_evidence.label: Phase-of-flight recovered from text — maneuvering is 55% fatal
raw_evidence.content: Because phase_flt_spec is empty in this slice (a known limitation, ana_caveat_01), we recover phase signals from the narrative probable-cause text. Landing-phase mentions are by far the most common (6,940 events, 40.2% of cause-text coverage) but only 4.4% fatal — most landing accidents are low-speed and survivable. Takeoff mentions: 2,628 events, 17.9% fatal. Approach: 1,149, 21.3% fatal. The standout is maneuvering: just 815 mentions, but 55.1% of them are fatal — by far the most lethal phase, consistent with the long-recognized 'maneuvering at low altitude in a stall-friendly attitude' fatal-accident pattern. Cruise mentions are surprisingly rare (265, 1.5%) — most GA accidents happen near the ground, not in steady cruise flight.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_22 ===")
phase_pats = {k: patterns[k] for k in patterns if k.startswith("phase_")}
prows = []
for name, pat in phase_pats.items():
    rx = re.compile(pat)
    hit = events_with_cause["cause"].str.contains(rx, regex=True)
    n = int(hit.sum())
    fatal_n = int(events_with_cause.loc[hit, "fatal"].sum())
    prows.append({
        "phase_text_mention": name.replace("phase_", ""),
        "events": n,
        "events_pct_of_cause_text": round(n / total_with_cause * 100, 1),
        "fatal_events": fatal_n,
        "fatal_share_pct": round(fatal_n / n * 100, 1) if n else 0,
    })
ptbl = pd.DataFrame(prows).sort_values("events", ascending=False)
print(ptbl.to_string(index=False))

raw_evidence.label: Probable-cause keyword taxonomy — what investigators actually say killed people
raw_evidence.content: Mining the 17,254 events with NTSB-written probable-cause text (98.5% coverage) for canonical accident-pattern keywords gives a fatality-weighted ranking that closely matches the GA-safety-literature consensus (det_06). Loss of control: 1,646 events / 51.2% fatal / 1,431 deaths. Aerodynamic stall: 1,420 / 49.9% fatal / 1,179 deaths. Engine failure: 3,876 events / 12.7% fatal / 732 deaths (very common but mostly survivable). Spatial disorientation: 298 events / 95.0% fatal / 558 deaths — the highest fatality rate of any high-volume pattern, almost always lethal. Controlled flight into terrain: 103 / 84.5% / 169. Structural failure / in-flight breakup: 97 / 85.6% / 168. Alcohol or drug impairment: 161 / 82.0% / 194. Stall-spin combined: 235 / 82.1% / 313. The pattern is consistent: rare events kill almost everyone they touch (disorientation, structural failure, alcohol), common events kill a minority (engine failure, landing accidents).

"spin": r"\bspin(s|ned|ning)?\b",
    "fuel_exhaustion": r"fuel exhaustion|exhausted (?:the )?fuel|out of fuel",
    "fuel_starvation": r"fuel starvation|starved of fuel",
    "fuel_management": r"fuel (?:mis)?management|inadequate fuel",
    "engine_failure": r"engine failure|loss of engine power|partial loss of engine|engine malfunction",
    "vfr_into_imc": r"vfr (?:flight )?into (?:imc|instrument)|continued vfr flight into|continued visual flight into imc",
    "spatial_disorientation": r"spatial disorientation",
    "controlled_flight_into_terrain": r"controlled flight into terrain|cfit",
    "wire_strike": r"wire strike|struck (?:a |the )?wire|powerline",
    "bird_strike": r"bird strike|struck a bird",
    "icing": r"\bicing\b|airframe ice|carb(?:uretor)? ice",
    "go_around": r"go.?around",
    "runway_excursion": r"runway excursion|departed the runway|overran the runway|veered off the runway",
    "hard_landing": r"hard landing",
    "porpoise": r"porpois(e|ing)",
    "stall_spin": r"stall(\b.{0,20}\bspin)|stall/spin",
    "improper_decision": r"improper (?:decision|judgment)|inadequate decision",
    "pilot_inexperience": r"inexperience(?:d)?|insufficient (?:total )?experience",
    "alcohol_drugs": r"alcohol|impairment|drug",
    "midair_collision": r"mid.?air collision|midair collision",
    "structural_failure": r"structural failure|in.?flight breakup|in.?flight break.?up",
    # Phases recovered from text — recovers what phase_flt_spec lost:
    "phase_takeoff": r"\b(takeoff|take.?off|initial climb)\b",
    "phase_landing": r"\b(landing|touchdown|flare)\b",
    "phase_approach": r"\bapproach\b",
    "phase_cruise": r"\bcruise\b",
    "phase_maneuvering": r"\bmaneuver(?:ing|ed)?\b",
    "phase_taxi": r"\btaxi(?:ing|ed)?\b",
}

# Roll one row per event (use first non-null cause text per event).
ev = df.groupby("ev_id").agg(
    cause=("cause_lc", "first"),
    fatal=("fatal", "any"),
    deaths=("inj_tot_f", "max"),
).reset_index()
total_events = ev.shape[0]
events_with_cause = ev[ev["cause"].str.len() > 0]
total_with_cause = events_with_cause.shape[0]
print(f"events_total: {total_events}")
print(f"events_with_cause_text: {total_with_cause}")
print(f"cause_text_coverage_pct: {total_with_cause / total_events * 100:.1f}")

rows = []
for name, pat in patterns.items():
    rx = re.compile(pat)
    hit = events_with_cause["cause"].str.contains(rx, regex=True)
    n = int(hit.sum())
    fatal_n = int(events_with_cause.loc[hit, "fatal"].sum())
    deaths = int(events_with_cause.loc[hit, "deaths"].sum())
    pct = (n / total_with_cause * 100) if total_with_cause else 0.0
    fpct = (fatal_n / n * 100) if n else 0.0
    rows.append({
        "pattern": name,
        "events": n,
        "events_pct": round(pct, 1),
        "fatal_events": fatal_n,
        "fatal_share_pct": round(fpct, 1),
        "deaths_sum": deaths,
    })

cause_tbl = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("events", ascending=False)
print(cause_tbl.to_string(index=False))

# --- ana_21: VFR-into-IMC by text vs by columns (cross-check det_05) ---
print("=== ana_21 ===")
text_hits = events_with_cause["cause"].str.contains(r"vfr (?:flight )?into (?:imc|instrument)|continued vfr flight into|continued visual flight into imc", regex=True)

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: Why this story matters — the gap between flying-as-airline-passenger and flying-as-private-pilot
raw_evidence.content: U.S. commercial aviation is one of the safest forms of transportation ever engineered: the airlines have flown for years on end without a passenger fatality in the U.S. General aviation is a different story. A private pilot in a Cessna 172 is operating in a regulatory regime, training environment, weather-decision context, and maintenance economy that is meaningfully closer to driving a car than to riding on Delta. The gap matters for two reasons. First, it shapes public perception: small-plane crashes generate disproportionate local-news coverage relative to airline accidents because they are common enough to be regular and rare enough to still be newsworthy. Second, the regulatory and educational levers that fixed airline safety in the 1990s and 2000s (crew resource management, sophisticated simulator training, two-pilot crews, mandatory route planning) only partly map onto single-pilot light-aircraft operations. So the story this dataset can tell — what kills private pilots, where, in what airplanes, in what weather — is also the story of a safety problem that the easy fixes have already been applied to and which remains stubbornly resistant to the next wave of fixes.

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: Why this story matters — the gap between flying-as-airline-passenger and flying-as-private-pilot
raw_evidence.content: U.S. commercial aviation is one of the safest forms of transportation ever engineered: the airlines have flown for years on end without a passenger fatality in the U.S. General aviation is a different story. A private pilot in a Cessna 172 is operating in a regulatory regime, training environment, weather-decision context, and maintenance economy that is meaningfully closer to driving a car than to riding on Delta. The gap matters for two reasons. First, it shapes public perception: small-plane crashes generate disproportionate local-news coverage relative to airline accidents because they are common enough to be regular and rare enough to still be newsworthy. Second, the regulatory and educational levers that fixed airline safety in the 1990s and 2000s (crew resource management, sophisticated simulator training, two-pilot crews, mandatory route planning) only partly map onto single-pilot light-aircraft operations. So the story this dataset can tell — what kills private pilots, where, in what airplanes, in what weather — is also the story of a safety problem that the easy fixes have already been applied to and which remains stubbornly resistant to the next wave of fixes.

Loss of control: 1,646 events / 51.2% fatal / 1,431 deaths. Aerodynamic stall: 1,420 / 49.9% fatal / 1,179 deaths. Engine failure: 3,876 events / 12.7% fatal / 732 deaths (very common but mostly survivable). Spatial disorientation: 298 events / 95.0% fatal / 558 deaths — the highest fatality rate of any high-volume pattern, almost always lethal. Controlled flight into terrain: 103 / 84.5% / 169. Structural failure / in-flight breakup: 97 / 85.6% / 168. Alcohol or drug impairment: 161 / 82.0% / 194. Stall-spin combined: 235 / 82.1% / 313. raw_evidence.content: U.S. commercial aviation is one of the safest forms of transportation ever engineered: the airlines have flown for years on end without a passenger fatality in the U.S. General aviation is a different story. The gap matters for two reasons. First, it shapes public perception: small-plane crashes generate disproportionate local-news coverage relative to airline accidents because they are common enough to be regular and rare enough to still be newsworthy. Second, the regulatory and educational levers that fixed airline safety in the 1990s and 2000s (crew resource management, sophisticated simulator training, two-pilot crews, mandatory route planning) only partly map onto single-pilot light-aircraft operations. So the story this dataset can tell — what kills private pilots, where, in what airplanes, in what weather — is also the story of a safety problem that the easy fixes have already been applied to and which remains stubbornly resistant to the next wave of fixes.

raw_evidence.label: The deadliest single events — when one crash kills many
raw_evidence.content: The worst single event in the dataset is the 2016 Lockhart, Texas hot-air-balloon crash with 16 deaths — caused per NTSB by 'the pilot's pattern of poor decision-making' that continued the flight in fog and descended through clouds; the pilot was operating under FAA rules that did not require a medical certificate for commercial balloon pilots. Second is the 2019 Mokuleia, Hawaii skydiving-plane crash (11 deaths) caused by 'aggressive takeoff maneuver, which resulted in an accelerated stall.' Third is the 2019 ten-fatality twin-engine takeoff crash. These three events alone account for 37 deaths — a meaningful share of any single year. The narratives field is what makes them work as story material: each comes with the NTSB's own one-sentence probable-cause statement, which is more direct and credible than any reconstruction a reporter would write.

raw_evidence.label: Probable-cause keyword taxonomy — what investigators actually say killed people
raw_evidence.content: Mining the 17,254 events with NTSB-written probable-cause text (98.5% coverage) for canonical accident-pattern keywords gives a fatality-weighted ranking that closely matches the GA-safety-literature consensus (det_06). Loss of control: 1,646 events / 51.2% fatal / 1,431 deaths. Aerodynamic stall: 1,420 / 49.9% fatal / 1,179 deaths. Engine failure: 3,876 events / 12.7% fatal / 732 deaths (very common but mostly survivable). Spatial disorientation: 298 events / 95.0% fatal / 558 deaths — the highest fatality rate of any high-volume pattern, almost always lethal. Controlled flight into terrain: 103 / 84.5% / 169. Structural failure / in-flight breakup: 97 / 85.6% / 168. Alcohol or drug impairment: 161 / 82.0% / 194. Stall-spin combined: 235 / 82.1% / 313. The pattern is consistent: rare events kill almost everyone they touch (disorientation, structural failure, alcohol), common events kill a minority (engine failure, landing accidents).
raw_evidence.code:
"spin": r"\bspin(s|ned|ning)?\b",
    "fuel_exhaustion": r"fuel exhaustion|exhausted (?:the )?fuel|out of fuel",
    "fuel_starvation": r"fuel starvation|starved of fuel",
    "fuel_management": r"fuel (?:mis)?management|inadequate fuel",
    "engine_failure": r"engine failure|loss of engine power|partial loss of engine|engine malfunction",
    "vfr_into_imc": r"vfr (?:flight )?into (?:imc|instrument)|continued vfr flight into|continued visual flight into imc",
    "spatial_disorientation": r"spatial disorientation",
    "controlled_flight_into_terrain": r"controlled flight into terrain|cfit",
    "wire_strike": r"wire strike|struck (?:a |the )?wire|powerline",
    "bird_strike": r"bird strike|struck a bird",
    "icing": r"\bicing\b|airframe ice|carb(?:uretor)? ice",
    "go_around": r"go.?around",
    "runway_excursion": r"runway excursion|departed the runway|overran the runway|veered off the runway",
    "hard_landing": r"hard landing",
    "porpoise": r"porpois(e|ing)",
    "stall_spin": r"stall(\b.{0,20}\bspin)|stall/spin",
    "improper_decision": r"improper (?:decision|judgment)|inadequate decision",
    "pilot_inexperience": r"inexperience(?:d)?|insufficient (?:total )?experience",
    "alcohol_drugs": r"alcohol|impairment|drug",
    "midair_collision": r"mid.?air collision|midair collision",
    "structural_failure": r"structural failure|in.?flight breakup|in.?flight break.?up",
    # Phases recovered from text — recovers what phase_flt_spec lost:
    "phase_takeoff": r"\b(takeoff|take.?off|initial climb)\b",
    "phase_landing": r"\b(landing|touchdown|flare)\b",
    "phase_approach": r"\bapproach\b",
    "phase_cruise": r"\bcruise\b",
    "phase_maneuvering": r"\bmaneuver(?:ing|ed)?\b",
    "phase_taxi": r"\btaxi(?:ing|ed)?\b",
}

# Roll one row per event (use first non-null cause text per event).
ev = df.groupby("ev_id").agg(
    cause=("cause_lc", "first"),
    fatal=("fatal", "any"),
    deaths=("inj_tot_f", "max"),
).reset_index()
total_events = ev.shape[0]
events_with_cause = ev[ev["cause"].str.len() > 0]
total_with_cause = events_with_cause.shape[0]
print(f"events_total: {total_events}")
print(f"events_with_cause_text: {total_with_cause}")
print(f"cause_text_coverage_pct: {total_with_cause / total_events * 100:.1f}")

rows = []
for name, pat in patterns.items():
    rx = re.compile(pat)
    hit = events_with_cause["cause"].str.contains(rx, regex=True)
    n = int(hit.sum())
    fatal_n = int(events_with_cause.loc[hit, "fatal"].sum())
    deaths = int(events_with_cause.loc[hit, "deaths"].sum())
    pct = (n / total_with_cause * 100) if total_with_cause else 0.0
    fpct = (fatal_n / n * 100) if n else 0.0
    rows.append({
        "pattern": name,
        "events": n,
        "events_pct": round(pct, 1),
        "fatal_events": fatal_n,
        "fatal_share_pct": round(fpct, 1),
        "deaths_sum": deaths,
    })

cause_tbl = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("events", ascending=False)
print(cause_tbl.to_string(index=False))

raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.

raw_evidence.label: Why this story matters — the gap between flying-as-airline-passenger and flying-as-private-pilot
raw_evidence.content: U.S. commercial aviation is one of the safest forms of transportation ever engineered: the airlines have flown for years on end without a passenger fatality in the U.S. General aviation is a different story. A private pilot in a Cessna 172 is operating in a regulatory regime, training environment, weather-decision context, and maintenance economy that is meaningfully closer to driving a car than to riding on Delta. The gap matters for two reasons. First, it shapes public perception: small-plane crashes generate disproportionate local-news coverage relative to airline accidents because they are common enough to be regular and rare enough to still be newsworthy. Second, the regulatory and educational levers that fixed airline safety in the 1990s and 2000s (crew resource management, sophisticated simulator training, two-pilot crews, mandatory route planning) only partly map onto single-pilot light-aircraft operations. So the story this dataset can tell — what kills private pilots, where, in what airplanes, in what weather — is also the story of a safety problem that the easy fixes have already been applied to and which remains stubbornly resistant to the next wave of fixes.

raw_evidence.label: Probable-cause keyword taxonomy — what investigators actually say killed people
raw_evidence.content: Mining the 17,254 events with NTSB-written probable-cause text (98.5% coverage) for canonical accident-pattern keywords gives a fatality-weighted ranking that closely matches the GA-safety-literature consensus (det_06). Loss of control: 1,646 events / 51.2% fatal / 1,431 deaths. Aerodynamic stall: 1,420 / 49.9% fatal / 1,179 deaths. Engine failure: 3,876 events / 12.7% fatal / 732 deaths (very common but mostly survivable). Spatial disorientation: 298 events / 95.0% fatal / 558 deaths — the highest fatality rate of any high-volume pattern, almost always lethal. Controlled flight into terrain: 103 / 84.5% / 169. Structural failure / in-flight breakup: 97 / 85.6% / 168. Alcohol or drug impairment: 161 / 82.0% / 194. Stall-spin combined: 235 / 82.1% / 313. The pattern is consistent: rare events kill almost everyone they touch (disorientation, structural failure, alcohol), common events kill a minority (engine failure, landing accidents).

    "engine_failure": r"engine failure|loss of engine power|partial loss of engine|engine malfunction",

    "bird_strike": r"bird strike|struck a bird",
    "icing": r"\bicing\b|airframe ice|carb(?:uretor)? ice",
    "go_around": r"go.?around",
    "runway_excursion": r"runway excursion|departed the runway|overran the runway|veered off the runway",
    "hard_landing": r"hard landing",
    "porpoise": r"porpois(e|ing)",
    "stall_spin": r"stall(\b.{0,20}\bspin)|stall/spin",
    "improper_decision": r"improper (?:decision|judgment)|inadequate decision",
    "pilot_inexperience": r"inexperience(?:d)?|insufficient (?:total )?experience",
    "alcohol_drugs": r"alcohol|impairment|drug",
    "midair_collision": r"mid.?air collision|midair collision",
    "structural_failure": r"structural failure|in.?flight breakup|in.?flight break.?up",
    # Phases recovered from text — recovers what phase_flt_spec lost:
    "phase_takeoff": r"\b(takeoff|take.?off|initial climb)\b",
    "phase_landing": r"\b(landing|touchdown|flare)\b",
    "phase_approach": r"\bapproach\b",
    "phase_cruise": r"\bcruise\b",
    "phase_maneuvering": r"\bmaneuver(?:ing|ed)?\b",
    "phase_taxi": r"\btaxi(?:ing|ed)?\b",
}

# Roll one row per event (use first non-null cause text per event).
ev = df.groupby("ev_id").agg(
    cause=("cause_lc", "first"),
    fatal=("fatal", "any"),
    deaths=("inj_tot_f", "max"),
).reset_index()
total_events = ev.shape[0]
events_with_cause = ev[ev["cause"].str.len() > 0]
total_with_cause = events_with_cause.shape[0]
print(f"events_total: {total_events}")
print(f"events_with_cause_text: {total_with_cause}")
print(f"cause_text_coverage_pct: {total_with_cause / total_events * 100:.1f}")

rows = []
for name, pat in patterns.items():
    rx = re.compile(pat)
    hit = events_with_cause["cause"].str.contains(rx, regex=True)
    n = int(hit.sum())
    fatal_n = int(events_with_cause.loc[hit, "fatal"].sum())
    deaths = int(events_with_cause.loc[hit, "deaths"].sum())
    pct = (n / total_with_cause * 100) if total_with_cause else 0.0

    rows.append({

        "events_pct": round(pct, 1),
        "fatal_events": fatal_n,
        "fatal_share_pct": round(fpct, 1),
        "deaths_sum": deaths,
    })

print(cause_tbl.to_string(index=False))

raw_evidence.content: U.S. commercial aviation is one of the safest forms of transportation ever engineered: the airlines have flown for years on end without a passenger fatality in the U.S. General aviation is a different story. The gap matters for two reasons. First, it shapes public perception: small-plane crashes generate disproportionate local-news coverage relative to airline accidents because they are common enough to be regular and rare enough to still be newsworthy. raw_evidence.label: Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) is the dominant fatal category
raw_evidence.content: Across the NTSB's modern reporting, Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I) — the airplane stops doing what the pilot is telling it to do while airborne, typically stall/spin — is the single largest source of fatal accidents in GA. It has been a fixture on the NTSB's Most Wanted List of safety improvements and is one of the General Aviation Joint Steering Committee's top focus areas. Many of the most-cited subcategories (VFR into IMC, base-to-final stalls during landing, maneuvering at low altitude) ultimately classify as LOC-I in the NTSB taxonomy. In this dataset, LOC-I will not be a single column — the Analyst will need to recognize it through phase_flt_spec (maneuvering, approach, climb) plus the language of narr_cause (which will say things like 'failure to maintain airspeed,' 'aerodynamic stall,' 'loss of control'). The narrative-text co-occurrence with structured fields is exactly the kind of place where a small grep through narr_cause can quantify what was previously qualitative.
